articles.title: How an attempt at Democratic unity exploded with Stevens’ Senate endorsement flip
articles.summary: As recently as Saturday night, the prospect of Democrat Haley Stevens endorsing Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan’s Senate race had seemed implausible.
articles.body:
As recently as Saturday night, the prospect of Democrat Haley Stevens endorsing Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan's Senate race had seemed implausible.

Stevens issued a statement praising Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed for saying he disagreed with a controversial advertisement that blamed the high cost of living in Michigan on the United States' aid to Israel. Despite a week of speculation about her withdrawing an endorsement for El-Sayed, her primary rival, she repeatedly said that she would do no such thing.

When staffers reached out last week to urge her not to endorse Rogers, Stevens replied in a text message, according to a person who saw the message: "Omg why would you think I would do that??!!"

At midnight Saturday, she told a key ally that she was sticking with El-Sayed. Then on Sunday morning, things changed.

She appeared at a Black church in Detroit with Rogers and then announced her change of heart to reporters gathered outside and on social media.

Her move stunned the political world — including Stevens' friends, colleagues and even her own congressional staffers, most of whom found out about her decision on social media and promptly quit, according to a statement from her chief of staff and people familiar with the matter.

The question that could decide Michigan's Senate race — and potentially, with it, which party will have majority control of the chamber for the last two years of Donald Trump's presidency — is whether Stevens' endorsement of Rogers will change votes or amount to more than political melodrama.

There have long been signs of discontent with El-Sayed within the Democratic coalition. Stevens was strongest in the August primary with Black and Jewish Democrats, some of whom have balked at supporting El-Sayed, a Muslim who is a strident critic of Israel's actions in Gaza and an advocate for ending foreign aid for Israel's military.

Prior to Stevens' defection, CNN's most recent poll of the Michigan Senate race had El-Sayed leading Rogers by seven points – with 95% support from Democratic likely voters. Already, Stevens' endorsement of Rogers is becoming something of a rally-around-the-flag moment for Democratic leaders — uniting a coalition in the race's final days around a shared sense of the stakes at hand.

Among the Democratic leaders who denounced Stevens and strongly backed El-Sayed were two of his most powerful intra-party critics: Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, who tacitly supported Stevens in the primary, and former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, who just days ago said El-Sayed's views on Israel were "wrong" and "more than concerning."

Schumer accused Stevens of a "despicable betrayal."

"Senate Democrats are united in our support for Abdul El-Sayed, because we know he will fight for the economic interests of working families in Michigan, unlike Mike Rogers, who is a tool of Donald Trump and billionaire donors," the New York Democrat said .

Schumer added that Democrats "are equally united in our total revulsion at the racist, Islamophobic, and over-the-top false attacks on Abdul by Republicans."

Pelosi, meanwhile, said on social media that El-Sayed "must win," and that Stevens "has chosen to dangerously betray Michigan families' healthcare, freedoms and future with her horrific endorsement of Mike Rogers."

As Stevens and Rogers spoke to reporters outside the church after the service, an individual in the crowd shouted: "Haley's a traitor!"

An El-Sayed campaign spokesperson said he raised $2.4 million on Sunday after Stevens endorsed Rogers — marking his "biggest fundraising day yet."

In an interview Sunday night with CNN's Anderson Cooper, Stevens said that endorsing Rogers was "just a weight off my shoulders." But she struggled to answer questions about why she'd changed her mind.

"Abdul has been getting angrier and angrier," Stevens said. "There are so many Democrats who want to vote for our Democratic nominee, and they're just being told, 'Hey, this is a party you don't belong in, or this is a campaign you don't belong in.'"

What she didn't explain, despite being asked several times, was what had changed between Saturday — when she told several Democrats she intended to appear with El-Sayed and Clyburn at church — and Sunday morning, when she instead went to a Detroit church with Rogers and endorsed him.

She said she was tired of watching El-Sayed stand with Hasan Piker — but didn't address the reality that El-Sayed's campaign appearances with Piker came before the primary election, and Stevens had endorsed El-Sayed after that primary's conclusion.

"I'm just sick of the people he stands with," Stevens said.

Michigan Rep. Debbie Dingell, a Democrat who had told CNN Sunday that Stevens reassured her Saturday that she wasn't switching sides, reacted by saying: "That was one of the most painful interviews I have ever watched."

Shortly after their primary, which El-Sayed won by less than a percentage point, the two hugged at a state party unity breakfast. But they had not campaigned together in months – or spoken directly during that time, as CNN reported last week.

Democrats attempted to negotiate a joint appearance Sunday at a Black church in Detroit alongside South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn, one of the party's most influential figures. The goal was to shore up Black support for El-Sayed.

One longtime Michigan Democratic operative said many older Black voters tend to cast their ballots on Election Day, rather than voting early, "because of a well-earned higher skepticism of absentee voting." Those votes could be an essential piece of the Democratic coalition El-Sayed is trying to hold together.

Stevens said in a statement Friday morning that Clyburn, who endorsed and campaigned with her in the primary, had invited her to the church — and that she would be attending, marking the first time she would appear jointly with El-Sayed on the campaign trail.

However, she also issued a list of demands for El-Sayed — including attempting to pressure him into denouncing an outside group's new advertisement that blamed the United States' foreign aid for Israel for Americans' struggles with high costs. The ad features two people in a grocery store suggesting they can't afford basic goods due to the aid. It echoed what El-Sayed has often said on the campaign trail about Israel, even as he distanced himself from the ad.

El-Sayed responded in a statement Friday night that Stevens "seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago."

It became clear that the joint appearance wouldn't happen late Friday, when CNN and other outlets reported that El-Sayed's campaign had asked Stevens to skip all campaign events in the race's closing days. Dingell said on CNN Saturday that she was the one who delivered the message to Stevens.

Still, on Saturday, El-Sayed denounced the ad, and Stevens issued a statement praising him for doing so — developments that made her decision Sunday more of a head-scratcher to many Democrats close to her. Dingell told CNN Sunday that Stevens had reassured her overnight that she wasn't switching sides.

Standing next to Rogers on Sunday, Stevens mentioned four times that El-Sayed's campaign had excluded her from his events. She pointed to it again in her endorsement video posted on X, noting El-Sayed "had said that I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away. And he's right."

"My vote for Senate is going to be with Mike Rogers, and I will tell you why. Because we have to stand with country. We can't stand with hate. We can't stand with Hasan Piker," she said.

Party officials moved swiftly on Sunday to publicly condemn Stevens and criticize her focus on being uninvited. But they privately said there was blame to go around — notably for El-Sayed.

"He acted like he won the primary in a landslide, but he didn't," one longtime Democratic official told CNN. "Abdul gave himself his own October surprise."

El-Sayed went ahead Sunday with the event. After asking reporters to focus on questions about issues facing people in his state rather than "two folks who aren't here right now," El-Sayed was asked if he believed Stevens had betrayed his party by backing Rogers.

"At the end of the day, I actually don't think about Haley Stevens," he said, standing next to Clyburn. "I think about, like I said, the 9,999,998 people who are not those two. Because you know what? I'm just less interested in the politics of it all than I am in the policy of it all."

A deeply emotional argument for many in the Democratic Party became particularly personal for El-Sayed and Stevens, both of whom are known for not listening much to advisers and following their own instincts.

Stevens was backed in the primary by tens of millions of dollars in spending from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee — a flashpoint between her and El-Sayed, who denounced AIPAC and the influence of money in politics at nearly every campaign event. El-Sayed was criticized for campaigning with Piker, the stridently pro-Palestinian live-streamer with a long history of controversial comments about Jews, including comparing Jewish residents who oppose El-Sayed to members of the Ku Klux Klan, remarks widely denounced as antisemitic. AIPAC on X reshared Stevens' video on Sunday endorsing Rogers.

During the primary, El-Sayed portrayed Stevens as an AIPAC puppet and called her "the least capable candidate in America."

"Everyone in America understands you want to blame all of your problems on Jewish Americans," Stevens responded on X days before the August 4 election .

As AIPAC's allied groups boosted her campaign, the animosity grew too. El-Sayed's multiple shots at Stevens as being a puppet angered her and made her dig in. Meanwhile, she was rankled by his repeated refusal to affirm that Israel had a right to exist as a Jewish state and his statements that it was committing genocide in Gaza and that funding to the country was hurting Michiganders.

Many of Stevens' Democratic critics on Sunday blamed Stevens' fiancé, Michigan lawyer Jason Turkish, who endorsed Rogers last week and did media interviews criticizing El-Sayed as uncommitted to Jewish safety.

One former Stevens staffer noted Sunday that after she and Turkish became engaged in May — something they kept private until after the August primary — Stevens grew more focused on defending Israel and AIPAC, even as the Democratic Party and US public opinion as a whole has become more skeptical of Israel. In the ex-staffer's view, she was speaking less about the message she'd run on and won with before: growing Michigan's economy and protecting manufacturing.

The topic often came up while preparing for interviews or donor calls, the staffer said. Preparing for a June interview, Stevens pressed aides on why she should avoid defending AIPAC when she had done so in a 2022 House primary against former Rep. Andy Levin and won.

Speculation about Turkish's influence burst into the open on Sunday, as Democrats — many of whom had either spoken to Stevens recently or been briefed by people who had — suggested he was playing an outsized role for a candidate's partner.

Former Pennsylvania Rep. Susan Wild, who in 2023 was Stevens' roommate in Washington and whose children regularly text with Stevens, said she was "terribly sad and disappointed" by her friend's "appalling" move.

"If this is because of her new relationship (about which many of us were so happy for her after she lost the primary), all I can say is that any woman who abandons her friends when a new guy comes along is no friend at all," Wild said.

Stevens' mother, Maria Marcotte, a retired advertising executive, told CNN in a statement that her daughter's fiancé had nothing to do with the change of heart — and that Marcotte herself had also voted for Rogers.

"Haley is her own woman. She always has been. Suggesting a man made her decision for her is insulting to her, and it is insulting to me as her mother," Marcotte said.

She pointed to episodes in which progressive pro-Palestinian activists hounded Stevens during the primary campaign.

"Abdul should not have thrown her out of the campaign for speaking her truth," she said. "Haley made this choice herself, with her eyes open, the way she has made every hard choice in her life. And I know Haley will support whoever wins this election, because that is who she is. I have never been prouder of her."

The anger between the two rivals kept growing from a distance after El-Sayed won the primary.

El-Sayed grouped Stevens in with all those he decided he didn't need to build his coalition after his primary victory. Stevens would tell people that she thought he was running a weird and losing campaign, but that she didn't feel it was her obligation to fix it.

Rogers aides, aware that his path to victory largely depended on a Democratic civil war, restrained themselves to spreading word of discontent and convincing themselves they weren't just fantasizing that they could get her all the way to endorsing.

Then came the grocery-store ad that rekindled the tension. It was released by a group linked to Cenk Uygur, co-creator of The Young Turks and — in a twist practically designed to create acrimony — Piker's uncle.

As Stevens demanded he denounce Uygur's ad, El-Sayed returned to name-checking AIPAC in his statement criticizing Stevens, something Michigan attorney general Dana Nessel, a Stevens primary backer who has raised concerns about Jewish safety, asked him to stop doing before she endorsed him. Nessel told CNN in October that El-Sayed had agreed to her request.

Stevens' defection threatened to worsen El-Sayed's standing with Jewish voters. Rogers has already predicted publicly that he could win as much as half the Jewish vote on Tuesday.

"It feels like over the last eight weeks, Dr. El-Sayed has become more egregious in the language he's been using," said Rabbi Aaron Starr, the president of the Michigan Board of Rabbis and a leader of the "Nonnegotiable" group of Jewish leaders. That group calls on El-Sayed to do more about concerns regarding Jewish safety and to affirm Jewish sovereignty in Israel. Starr and other Jewish leaders held a call Sunday afternoon to discuss the endorsement flip.

But Stevens was also damaged with key allies.

Dingell, long a peacemaker within the state party, chided Stevens' "continued efforts to get attention."

"Unfortunately, she's seriously hurt herself," Dingell told CNN.

Curtis Hertel, the chairman of the Michigan Democratic Party, effectively booted Stevens from it. He wrote on social media: "Congresswoman Stevens is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future."

Many Democrats in the state felt that for most of the preceding year, Stevens was viable in the Senate race largely because she'd cornered Schumer into effectively backing her. Into the spring, complaints circulated about what a lackluster primary campaign she was running, how much she was struggling on the stump, and how she was lashing out against those who wouldn't support her.

Despite her eventual strength with African American voters, Black church leaders were angry about her efforts to push for early endorsements. Chokwe Pitchford, a 27-year-old district commissioner from Benton Harbor and seen as a local rising star, told a story that he says encapsulated the kind of experience other Michigan Democrats he knows had: One morning, he discovered a graphic online from Stevens saying he'd endorsed her, even though as he posted in response, they'd never spoken.

"Instead of reaching out and apologizing, I had people from around the state calling from unknown numbers saying my political career is over if I don't take that down," Pitchford told CNN. "Some of us tried to ring this alarm bell a year ago; there was a problem here."

Indeed, the most robust praise for Stevens on Sunday was coming from Republicans.

"Haley said what few people are willing to say. She showed great and almost unprecedented loyalty to the Great People of Michigan with what she did," Trump wrote on Truth Social.

The story and headline have been updated with additional information.

Todd reported from Detroit. CNN's Dana Bash, Manu Raju, Nicky Robertson and Jeff Zeleny contributed to this report.

articles.title: Xavier Becerra’s ‘California dream’ faces reality check as governor’s mansion beckons
articles.summary: Former US representative, health secretary and state attorney general is a shoo-in after a stunning comeback victory in primary
articles.body:
It was Tuesday, and the man poised to be the next governor of California wanted to talk about Donald Trump .

Xavier Becerra had come to Guelaguetza restaurant in Los Angeles to talk about Trump's attacks on voting in the state, but instead found himself answering questions about a presidential provocation of a different order.

The previous day, Trump had addressed a crowd in Nebraska , and at some point during the nearly two-hour speech the president had suggested, perhaps in jest but with enough specificity to rattle nerves, that Iran might "take out" Los Angeles and San Diego.

"Life is already tough enough in California," Becerra, 68, told reporters at the No on Prop 39 campaign event that Tuesday, offering his reaction only after taking questions related to the voter ID ballot measure being pushed by Trump's allies in the state. "You don't need to have a president pile on and say, 'I don't care about you. If you get bombed, who cares?'"

Should Becerra win, as he is all but certain to do in the heavily Democratic state, his first two years in the governor's office will coincide with the final two years of Trump's presidency.

Tangling with Trump is hardly new territory for Becerra. As the state's attorney general during the president's first term, he sued the Trump administration more than 100 times. Under priorities on Becerra's campaign website, "fighting Donald Trump" is listed second behind "healthcare".

Trump has spent nearly a decade targeting California, its laws and its leaders. But many of the state's deeper structural challenges predate his political rise.

California remains prohibitively expensive. Owning a home is out of reach for millions of residents, and for those who do own one, higher wildfire risk makes insurance harder to get – and keep. Housing, utility and fuel costs run well above the national average. Hollywood is struggling, and residents are increasingly at odds with the tech titans driving the AI boom from the north of the state.

"All you ever say is 'Trump, Trump, Trump,'" Becerra's Republican opponent, Steve Hilton, charged in their sole general election debate . "That's nothing but an insult to every Californian who is desperate for something to change in this state."

Californians head to the polls in an exceptionally pessimistic mood, according to a new survey by the Public Policy Institute of California. More than eight in 10 say the country is headed in the wrong direction, and nearly six in 10 say the same of the state. Just two in 10 Californians approve of Trump's performance in office – a record low across both terms of his presidency.

That leaves the next governor with the same weighty mandate handed to his predecessor, Gavin Newsom: lead the resistance to Trump's Washington while delivering relief at home.

"It's going to be a tough political environment for the new governor," said Mark Baldassare, survey director at the Public Policy Institute of California. "People are feeling a real sense of urgency about the need to do something about affordability, the prices, cost of housing, the cost of energy … I'm not sure there's going to be much of a honeymoon."

Understated and amiable, Becerra is running on a gauzy promise to restore the " California dream " that allowed the son of Mexican immigrants to blaze a path from a one-room apartment in Sacramento, where he was raised alongside three sisters, to Stanford Law School, the California state assembly and then Congress.

He was elected to House of Representatives in 1992, at 34,amid a wave of Latino political activism in the state. He served 12 terms as a member of the US House representing central Los Angeles. As a member of House Democratic leadership, he helped draft and pass the Affordable Care Act, the Obama-era law that dramatically expanded access to health insurance coverage.

After nearly a quarter-century in Washington, Becerra surprised the political establishment on both coasts by returning to Sacramento, the state's capital, to become the first Latino attorney general of California, succeeding Kamala Harris after she was elected to the US Senate. It put him at the vanguard of California's clash with Trump.

"While we don't go looking for a fight, we're prepared to act when the people, resources and values of California are at stake," Becerra said at the time, announcing the state's 100th lawsuit against the Trump administration.

In the midst of the surging coronavirus pandemic, Becerra returned to Washington to serve as the nation's health secretary under Joe Biden.

Not so long ago, it seemed that his political ascent might end there. His campaign for governor stalled soon after it launched – first, eclipsed by the prospect of a Kamala Harris run and then overlooked as Democrats searched for seemingly anyone else.

"When we started this campaign, we were the underdogs," Becerra said at a rally in Hollywood on the eve of the election. "Actually we were an afterthought, maybe even a punchline."

Fear began to spread that the party was running out of time to unite behind Newsom's would-be successor and that the presence of too many Democrats with middling support might allow two Republicans to advance to the general election under the state's non-partisan primary system. In short, the party was suggesting that he should drop out.

Becerra, once described by longtime California political columnist George Skelton as someone who "excels at being in the right place at the right time", stuck around. When the gubernatorial campaign of Eric Swalwell, the now former California congressman, imploded amid allegations of sexual misconduct, the afterthought became the frontrunner.

Becerra spent the rest of the turbulent primary campaign brawling with Tom Steyer, a progressive who backed Medicare for All and higher taxes on ultra-wealthy Californians like himself.

Steyer spent record sums and attacked Becerra's corporate ties. But he was a billionaire spending hundreds of millions of dollars to drown out his opponents at a moment when voters, particularly on the left, were deeply skeptical of both.

Becerra ran on his résumé, even as Democrats across the country turned to anti-establishment populists and insurgents angry at the system. He had passed bills and whipped votes; run an executive agency with a budget larger than the US military; and sued Trump again and again. In short, he knew the levers to pull to help the Golden state get its shine back.

Critics argued that the résumé looked less impressive in practice. Former Biden administration officials came forward with sharp criticism of Becerra's nearly four-year tenure at the Department of Health and Human Services. His detractors recalled a weak leader who had been all-but " invisible " as the federal administration marshaled a response to the pandemic – a charge Becerra pushed back on at the time. Others criticized his handling of the child migration crisis.

Former Becerra staffers bristle at that characterization of their boss's leadership, instead portraying him as a "deliberative" and "methodical" negotiator who sought out diverse viewpoints and prized progress over purity.

"He always remembers where he came from," Sirat Attapit, who worked for Becerra on Capitol Hill and in the state attorney general's office, said. "His north star really is his parents."

The test he applied to policy, she said, was personal: "Does this help people like my parents? Does it make life just a little bit easier for people like them?"

Voters picked him. And Hilton, with Trump's endorsement, advanced to the second-place spot, edging out Steyer.

In a state that has elected actors and presidential aspirants – and in the case of Ronald Reagan, both – Becerra is, by his own admission , "not the slickest" candidate to ever seek the governor's mansion.

A father to three daughters who flaunts his Costco membership, the Los Angeles Times columnist Gustavo Arellano dubbed Becerra a " Chicano Ned Flanders ". Like Biden did when he ran for president six years ago, Becerra offers steadiness and experience.

To date, the 68-year-old has given no indication that he views the governorship as a waypoint to the presidency.

Mark Gonzalez, a Democratic state assembly member who first met Becerra as a high school student, when Becerra was his congressman, said California needed a leader with his temperament – "someone calm, even-keeled and collected to be able to go into this storm that we're calling the Trump administration".

"You're not a movie star," he said. "You're the governor of California."

The knock on Becerra is that his agenda is too vague. Critics say his plans are aspirational but lack detail, while progressives fear an establishmentarian who fails to recognize the scale of change required of this moment.

"I would prefer not to run on inflated promises that then I can't deliver on," Becerra has said .

As governor, Becerra says lowering costs and expanding healthcare would be his top priorities. He wants to reduce permitting times for housing construction, expand down-payment assistance for first-time homebuyers, and has vowed to declare a state of emergency to address the housing shortage. He recently proposed a "power hour" of free midday electricity for low-income households.

Becerra says he supports " real guardrails " on artificial intelligence to protect workers and children, and believes Californians should share in the prosperity generated by leading tech companies that have made the state their home. But he hasn't outlined exactly what that would look like.

"He has no incentive now to be specific," said Melissa Michelson, a political science professor at Menlo College.

Polls show Becerra with a predictably wide lead over Hilton, in the state where Democrats hold a roughly two-to-one voter advantage over Republicans. It is to Becerra's advantage, Michelson said, to wait and see what the fiscal and political landscape looks like after the election, rather than propose a suite of policies that might prove unfeasible once in office.

"Obviously, it's frustrating to folks who want to know what's going to happen," she said. "But politically, it's a very logical strategy."

Becerra's ambitions will be set against what analysts warn is a long-term structural deficit . Heavy reliance on AI-driven growth and tax revenue from the ultra-rich has left the state's budget exposed to fiscal volatility, they say.

Compounding those fiscal pressures is the near-term risk posed by a hostile White House. Survivors of the Los Angeles fires in 2025 are still waiting for federal disaster aid, while communities rattled by immigration raids grapple with the aftershocks of mass arrests and deportations. Tariffs and the war in Iran have driven up costs everywhere, as the state braces for a sharp rise in its uninsured rate after the healthcare cuts approved under Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act take effect next year . And in the final weeks before the 3 November midterm elections, the Trump administration has escalated its attacks on California's elections system, alleging voter fraud.

One proposal to offset the looming coverage losses is the ballot measure known as Proposition 40 – a one-time 5% wealth tax on Californians worth more than $1bn. The so-called billionaire tax, brought to the ballot by a healthcare union and championed by the progressive senator Bernie Sanders, could raise huge sums earmarked primarily for healthcare. But it faces opposition from an unlikely coalition that includes Becerra, Newsom, tech billionaires, the California Teachers Association and Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California.

Billionaires should pay more, Becerra has said, but Prop 40 is "not the way to do tax policy".

After winning the primary in June, Becerra kept a relatively low profile. So low, in fact, that when comedian Sophia Garrow interviewed him for the San Francisco Standard , she asked if he knew who he was running against in November. The confusion, she said, stemmed from the fact that Becerra's website was still filled with references to Steyer months after his rival exited the race. (It has since been updated.)

In the final stretch, Becerra stepped up his campaigning, crisscrossing the state to rally for Democratic candidates running in competitive House seats redrawn last year as part of California's counterpunch to Texas's gerrymander. On Sunday night, he dropped back down to Los Angeles for a rally with Newsom, Harris and the state's US senators, Democrats Alex Padilla and Adam Schiff.

"In so many ways, this election is a choice between reaching higher for California's golden dream or descending further down Donald Trump's golden infamous escalator," the Democratic nominee told an ebullient crowd, waving "Becerra era" placards. "I promise California will be the light at the end of the tunnel for the next two years."

On the campaign trail, Becerra frequently invokes his parents, retelling the story of their arrival in California from Mexico "with just $12 in their pockets". Yet he has not made much of what his historic victory would mean in a state where more than 40% of residents are Latino and nearly one in two children has an immigrant parent.

No Latino has been elected governor of California in modern times. The last time was in 1875, when the then lieutenant governor, Romualdo Pacheco , served the remaining months of the governor's term.

In Los Angeles last month, surrounded at the anti-Proposition 39 event by Congressman Pete Aguilar, chair of the House Democratic caucus, and Monique Limón, state senate president pro tempore, Becerra reflected, briefly, on the ascendancy of Latino political power in the 30 years since California voters overwhelming approved Proposition 187 , a law that would have denied public services to undocumented immigrants, but was ultimately ruled unconstitutional.

"It's not because we got lucky," Becerra said. "It's not because it was accidental. It was very intentional. There was a lot of hard work done by our parents, by our communities, to get us where we are."

Part of his final push this campaign season is to defeat Prop 39, a ballot initiative that would require additional identification to vote.

Making his case in English and Spanish, Becerra spoke of his mother, a naturalized US citizen.

"We want to make it possible for people to exercise their vote," he said. "I want to make sure I protect my mother's right to vote."

articles.title: Supreme Court denies Trump admin request to reverse block on segregating 20K California ballots
articles.summary: The Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration's request to segregate more than 20,000 California mail-in ballots flagged for potential noncitizen voting.
articles.body: The U.S. Supreme Court (SCOTUS) on Monday rejected a Trump administration request to temporarily block lower-court rulings that denied requests to segregate more than 20,000 California mail-in ballots cast by people it says are likely not U.S. citizens. Justice Elena Kagan denied the appeal on the eve of the midterm elections without comment, and did not refer it to the other justices. The administration argued that the limited injunction would preserve the ballots while their eligibility is investigated, without canceling any votes. California and the federal government dispute whether the ballots are unlawful. "Once illegally cast ballots are counted and commingled with lawful votes, the resulting harm is impossible to remedy," the Department of Justice (DOJ) wrote in a court filing. JUDGE REJECTS DOJ REQUEST TO BLOCK CALIFORNIA FROM IMMEDIATELY COUNTING BALLOTS LINKED TO ALLEGED NONCITIZENS The SCOTUS appeal came about after the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals rejected the request Friday, with Judge Patrick Bumatay dissenting, as did a federal judge in Los Angeles last week. The DOJ sought relief while the matter proceeds. California says its safeguards against noncitizen voting are robust and argues the federal list may contain errors that could disenfranchise eligible voters. The lower courts also cited the state’s authority over election procedures and warned that granting the request could jeopardize the election. On Monday evening, a federal judge in Washington, D.C., said it was "likely" the Trump administration violated the Constitution by taking over responsibilities for elections from the states and Congress. Chief Judge James Boasberg issued an injunction blocking the administration from making requests from California over its mail-in ballots. DOJ HAS VERIFIED 20,000 NONCITIZENS ON CALIFORNIA VOTER ROLLS, FEDERAL PROSECUTOR SAYS The case stems from an Oct. 15 DOJ lawsuit alleging that California is impeding enforcement of a federal law barring noncitizens from voting in federal elections. The administration says the state violated the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause, which generally gives federal law precedence over state law. The dispute comes amid the administration’s broader push to influence how states run elections, including demands for access to voter rolls and warnings that officials could face prosecution for knowingly allowing noncitizens to vote. Fox News' Shannon Bream and Bill Mears and Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: Complaint filed against all 122 judges in Colorado election
articles.summary: (The Center Square) - With the general election just one day away, all 122 Colorado judges on the ballot are named in a former state official's request for j...
articles.body:
(The Center Square) - With the general election just one day away, all 122 Colorado judges on the ballot are named in a former state official's request for judicial misconduct investigations.

Christopher Gregory, the former executive director of the Colorado Commission on Judicial Discipline, on Sunday evening filed a "Request for Evaluation" with the same commission for all of the judges. Gregory alleged the judges had knowledge of judicial misconduct – whether their own or a colleague's. Gregory also alleged the state Judicial Performance Commission intentionally misled voters in its evaluations of the judges ahead of the 2026 general election.

All of the judges in Tuesday's election are being considered for retention, a process in which Coloradans will vote on whether each judge continues at the bench.

Gregory asserted each judge knowingly concealed material information from voters.

"Not a single judge subject to retention came forward to object to the legal adequacy, accuracy and completeness of the 2026 judicial performance evaluation reports," Gregory wrote in his complaint.

Gregory referred to a 2025 Colorado law that requires the performance commission to evaluate judicial integrity. He contended that all 25 performance commissions within the state and each judicial district failed to adequately consider allegations involving missing personal financial disclosures, a controversial 2019 judicial branch contract and the private discipline of an Adams County judge accused of an inappropriate sexual relationship with court staff.

Gregory argued that the judges, in failing to publicly challenge the performance evaluation process and commission, violated judicial ethics rules that have not been adjudicated.

The Center Square reached out to the 122 judges, the state's judicial branch, and the judicial performance and discipline commissions. They did not respond in time for publication.

Gregory has filed over 45 civil protection order petitions and a variety of other motions and complaints against several high-level state officials and independent commissions, including Attorney General Phil Weiser, a Democrat who's running for governor against Republican Victor Marx. The Center Square reached out to Weiser's office, but spokesperson Lawrence Pacheco declined to comment on Gregory's filings, including Sunday evening's complaint.

Justice William Hood, who is up for retention for the Colorado Supreme Court, and four judges on the ballot for the Court of Appeals – Rebecca Freyre, Elizabeth Harris, Katharine Lum and Grant Sullivan – were named in Gregory's July 2026 lawsuit against every judicial performance commission in the state. He filed the lawsuit in Denver County Court but named all of the commissions, alleging they failed to give voters complete and accurate information about judges standing for retention.

Another six judges – four county court and two district court judges – were also named in the July performance evaluations lawsuit.

Denver County has its own performance commission that has sole jurisdiction over the county's judges. Gregory told The Center Square he filed another request for evaluation for the seven judges facing retention there on Monday morning with the county performance commission

Gregory alleged that some of the judges had not filed their personal finance statements, which is required by Colorado law, and that others had "known [or] reasonably suspected judicial and attorney misconduct of their colleagues."

Adams County Court Judge Leroy Kirby was among the list of judges who Gregory said had not filed his personal finance statements. Gregory said Kirby was also the unnamed judge that Gregory identified in his June 2026 response to an emergency motion to seal – a document that was sent to every member of the Colorado General Assembly (the Legislature), all statewide candidates and news outlets – as having an inappropriate sexual relationship with court staff in the courthouse.

Fewer than five legislators or candidates responded to the publicly circulated document, and no media outlets pursued coverage, according to Gregory.

Kirby had "a duty to self-report his judicial misconduct and dishonesty when he applied for the 17th Judicial District Court in 2019 and when he stood for retention in 2024," Gregory said.

Kirby has not responded to The Center Square's inquiries for comments about the allegations.

Gregory told The Center Square that he served as the vice chair of the discipline commission in 2019 when Kirby received the private disciplinary action. And when Kirby was up for retention in 2024, he did not disclose his previous disciplinary action or his nondisclosure of personal finance statements in 2019 to the nominating commission, Gregory said. He also did not tell the discipline commission about his disciplinary history when applying for the Adams County district court judge in 2019, according to Gregory.

The misconduct by the other judges' behalf is regarding their "material omissions by failing to object to the 2026 judicial performance evaluation reports" that were "legally inaccurate and incomplete," Gregory said.

He also said the Colorado Judicial Performance Commission is blindly leading voters yet again ahead of the 2026 election by not fulfilling its legally required duties to evaluate judicial integrity. Gregory asserted that hiding material information falls under the umbrella of "dishonesty."

"All of the judges have mandatory reporting obligations when they are aware of their own or a colleague's substantial misconduct," Gregory told The Center Square.

"Here, everyone has remained silent about the problems with the judicial performance evaluations," Gregory said in his filing, and noted that none of the judges inquired about judicial integrity, the issues concerning the lack of judges' personal finance disclosures, Kirby's inappropriate relationship and the 2019 contract controversy in which a former chief of staff for the State Judicial Administrator's Office was allegedly offered a contract in exchange for not filing a sexual discrimination lawsuit.

Bill DeLisio, the Colorado Judicial Performance Commission's deputy director, previously told The Center Square that the commission looks at the judges' integrity and considers any disciplinary actions in its evaluation, as required by Colorado law. However, he said the commission did not consider an already completed investigation from the 2019 contract scandal that documented Hood and Sullivan's knowledge in their 2026 performance evaluations even though the commission may consider that information.

Gregory had brought up the fact that an anonymous letter was sent to Kent Wagner, the director the Judicial Performance Commission, on July 2, 2024, that requested an evaluation of judges facing retention who had allegedly failed to file required personal financial disclosures. Among that list of judges was Kirby, Gregory said.

The Center Square reached out to Wagner to confirm whether he received the letter and if he considered it in Kirby's evaluation, but he did not respond before publication.

The Center Square also reached out to the Secretary of State's Office to determine whether Secretary Jena Griswold, a Democrat running for attorney general in Tuesday's election against Republican Michael Allen, was aware of these judges' failure to file personal finance statements and whether action was taken against them, but Griswold did not respond. Judges are required to file such statements under Colorado Revised Statues § 24-6-202. That's a section of the Colorado Public Official Disclosure Law.

As part of his request Sunday, Gregory is asked to be recognized as an official complaint under Colorado law. He is also seeking that the disciplinary commission and staff "disqualify themselves, and for the Colorado Supreme Court to allow the formation of a special tribunal through a conflict-free selection process"

Gregory filed the request for a special tribunal on Oct. 13 with the Boulder County Court in Longmont. The respondent listed is Boulder County District Attorney Michael Dougherty, who currently faces separate litigation where Gregory is seeking to challenge his prosecutorial inaction and compel criminal prosecution for his allegations surrounding judicial misconduct coverup. Dougherty lost the Democratic primary for state attorney general race to Griswold.

articles.title: Forecasts of midterm blue wave put Trump’s legacy on line
articles.summary: President Trump’s political capital is on the line ahead of the midterm elections as a potential blue wave threatens his final two years in office. Trump has...
articles.body:
President Trump's political capital is on the line ahead of the midterm elections as a potential blue wave threatens his final two years in office.

Trump has crisscrossed the country, holding 28 in-person campaign rallies in addition to a series of tele-rallies. The president has made stops in Republican strongholds like Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas and even Alaska in an effort to keep the states firmly in the red column. He's also visited a number of deep-red states like Mississippi and South Carolina, where polls show closer than expected races.

While Trump has argued his rallies have boosted Republican incumbents and candidates in the states, recent polling suggests otherwise.

A New York Times/Siena poll released the day before Election Day showed Democrats with leads in Senate races in Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas and Alaska.

Trump's heavy political investment in the states means he could end up shouldering the blame for a potential blue wave, which could impact the GOP beyond Election Day.

Republicans warn that a blue wave would be detrimental to the last two years of the Trump administration, and by extension, his legacy.

"It impacts his ability to drive policy over the next two years, or if a Supreme Court nomination comes up, or fill in the blank in terms of even Cabinet turnover," said one Republican strategist, speaking on condition of anonymity. "All of that too will help shape his legacy, and it's how people remember you at the end that guides you into the history books."

In a statement to The Hill on Monday, the Republican National Committee (RNC) warned that Democrats would "obstruct" Trump's agenda and that their "disastrous economic policies" would drive jobs overseas.

"The president knows what's at stake this cycle, which is why he's barnstormed the country to encourage our voters to support Republican candidates that will advance his agenda and deliver for the American people," said RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre.

But during an election eve speech at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, Trump did not appear entirely focused on the elections that could impact the trajectory of his last two years in office.

The president spent the first 22 minutes of his 37-minute address — largely viewed as a closing message before the midterms — talking about his administration's efforts to repair the Reflecting Pool. Trump showed off a number of pre-renovation pictures of the pool and at one point invited Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to the podium to give brief remarks.

Trump also touted his numerous beautification projects and lower crime in the nation's capital.

Republican operative Rob Stutzman called Trump's speech "another Captain Queeg moment," a reference to a character from Herman Wouk's 1951 novel "The Caine Mutiny" who is considered an unstable and incompetent commander.

A second Republican strategist said, "What the utter f--- was that?" when asked for their reaction to Trump's speech at the Reflecting Pool.

"Republicans were hoping that he would have some sort of a closing message, some sort of American message with it, with a wonderful backdrop that could maybe be of help in the closing hours here," the unnamed GOP strategist said. "As we Republicans are losing touch with the public, it looked like he was losing touch with reality."

One national Republican operative noted the speech was "not surprising" considering Trump's communication style but expressed frustration with the closing message.

"This perfectly encapsulates his messaging throughout this entire campaign cycle, but it's deeply frustrating when we need to be laser-focused on turning out our low propensity voters tomorrow," the operative said.

A third Republican strategist defended the speech, arguing the Reflecting Pool was "a hook" for Trump to be able to talk about issues like crime and immigration.

"It's one of these things that wherever you get the opportunity to speak to a national audience, you're going to talk about the midterms even if you have to start with something else," the strategist said.

Trump did take some time during his speech Monday to urge Republicans to turn out on Election Day.

"If the people that voted for me and voted in the last election where we had such a great victory, if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide," the president said.

"Now, that doesn't happen because usually whoever the sitting president is — Republican or Democrat, good or bad, good president, great president, bad president — for some reason the sitting president doesn't win the midterms."

"We gave this a very strong shot," he added.

Much of the GOP's strategy has hinged on turning out its low-propensity base as much as possible, arguably a tall order for any political party in a nonpresidential election. Republicans hoped to defy that trend by dispatching Trump on the campaign trail, urging voters to "pretend" like he is on the ballot.

"The amount of rallies he did shows he 'believes' that he's on the ballot tomorrow," said Dan Eberhart, a Republican donor. "He worked hard, and he's right: Tomorrow's outcome is a reflection on him."

In a statement to The Hill, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle referred to Trump as the GOP's "best messenger" and "unmatched motivator" who is "committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress."

But some Republicans are unsure whether that tactic will ultimately work.

"So far from what we've seen, those rallies have not done what they were meant to do," said the first unnamed Republican strategist.

Democrats have been heartened by signs of early turnout in key battlegrounds, but Republicans argue that a large share of their voters tend to vote in person on Election Day.

"They're banking on these Republicans and the folks that he's trying to rally to show up tomorrow, and Republicans historically and should do exceedingly well tomorrow," the first Republican strategist said. "But the fact is, they still underperformed in places like Texas and in Florida in the early vote."

According to data released by Texas's secretary of State, 7.7 million voters in the Lone Star State voted early.

Meanwhile in Florida, registered Republicans led registered Democrats in early voting by just a little more than 200,000 voters. By comparison, in 2022, registered Republicans led Democrats in early voting by just a little less than 500,000 voters.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) on Sunday sounded the alarm over low turnout in the state, which has become known as a nerve center for Republican politics.

"If people stay home, you could end up seeing results that you're going to be wondering what happened. That's just the reality," DeSantis said at a campaign event.

"The reality is gas is higher, and that's not good. Some of these Republicans act like it's no big deal. I disagree with that. It is a big deal to people," the Florida governor continued.

articles.title: US senator wants 'full accounting' of Air Force One White House flyover
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, Nov 2 (Reuters) - US Senator Tammy Duckworth, the top Democrat on a subcommittee that oversees aviation regulation, asked government agencies on...
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump host a Halloween event at the White House

WASHINGTON, Nov 2 (Reuters) - US Senator Tammy Duckworth, the top Democrat on a subcommittee that oversees aviation regulation, asked government agencies on Monday for a full accounting of why they ‌allowed a White House flyover last week by the presidential airplane in what she said was a "dangerous ‌stunt."

The flyover, part of a children's Halloween party attended by President Donald Trump on Thursday, forced a temporary halt to traffic at ​Reagan Washington National Airport that delayed flights, while city lawmakers voiced concerns that residents, officials and the airport received only 15 minutes' notice.

Duckworth, an Illinois Democrat whose subcommittee oversees the Federal Aviation Administration, said flight-tracking data showed the aircraft made two passes on Thursday over the White House between roughly 400 and 1,000 feet (122 to 305 meters) and close ‌to the top of the Washington Monument.

She ⁠said the plane — a Qatari-donated interim presidential aircraft — was below the minimum safe altitude required by the FAA.

"A serious president would be bringing costs down," Duckworth wrote in a ⁠letter to the agencies. "This one is busy showing off his toys, putting on full display how wildly out of touch he is with the needs of the American people."

She asked the FAA, the Pentagon and the White House Office of ​Management ​and Budget to respond to detailed questions about the cost ​and limited public notice, while asking the Pentagon ‌if the flight was approved for training and what objective it might have achieved.

Duckworth also asked FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford when the agency was notified and what minimum altitude it authorized.

"The FAA followed all necessary protocols to ensure the safety of Washington, D.C. residents," the White House said, adding the flyover "brought joy and excitement to all those celebrating Halloween at the White House and to many nearby who got to enjoy the spectacle."

Trump is a ‌fan of Air Force One flyovers and they often happen ​at sporting events he is attending.

The Pentagon and FAA said they ​would respond directly to Duckworth. The FAA said ​the flight was coordinated with the agency.

The plane is designated Air Force One when Trump ‌is on board.

The District of Columbia city council ​said the limited notice of ​the flyover "startled many, including us."

Airline officials said they had less than an hour's notice.

Some people flying to Washington reported their planes were forced to circle or that they faced delays due to the flyover. ​FlightAware, a flight-tracking website, said 26% ‌of departing flights and 17% of arriving flights at Reagan National Airport were delayed on Thursday — or ​202 in total. Most of those delays were tied to the airport disruption.

(Reporting by David Shepardson, ​Editing by Franklin Paul, Rod Nickel and Edmund Klamann)

articles.title: War, tariffs and China: What the US midterms mean for the Asia-Pacific
articles.summary: Hit hard by Trump’s tariffs and the war on Iran, countries in the Asia-Pacific want ‘enormous changes’ in US policies.
articles.body:
Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia – Across the Asia-Pacific region, governments and businesses reeling from the energy shock of the United States and Israel’s war on Iran are watching Tuesday’s US midterm elections closely.

Many want to see “enormous changes” during the rest of President Donald Trump’s term, analysts say, from the war on Iran to his policies on trade and tariffs. But few expect that to happen, even with the Democrats poised to take the House of Representatives, and potentially the Senate, from Trump’s Republican Party.

“Of course, everybody is watching,” said Steven Okun, a trade specialist and the chief executive of APAC Advisors, a Singapore-based consulting firm. “It’s great political theatre.”

Outside the Middle East, no region has been hit harder by the war on Iran than the Asia-Pacific. Before the start of the conflict in January, the region took in most of the Gulf oil and gas that passed through the Strait of Hormuz.

When Iran closed the chokepoint in response to the US and Israel’s strikes, much of the region was left facing shortages .

The Philippines, which relies on the Gulf for more than 90 percent of its crude oil imports, has been under a national energy emergency since March. Soaring fuel costs have drained the foreign exchange reserves of the region’s poorest economies – Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar and East Timor, according to the Institute of Southeast Asian Studies (ISEAS)-Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore. Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam have also spent heavily on fuel subsidies to shield consumers, it said.

Public opinion in the US and the Asia-Pacific region remains firmly opposed to the war, but Okun said a Democratic-controlled US Congress was unlikely to force Trump to end the eight-month conflict.

“With Iran, I don’t see [a Democrat-controlled Congress] having much change at all, other than the fact that the war will be investigated and there will be oversight hearings,” Okun told Al Jazeera. “We might even see an impeachment of the secretary of defence, but it doesn’t change the overall impact of the war.”

Under the US Constitution, Congress holds the power to formally declare war, but Trump has claimed the attacks on Iran were in self-defence and has so far ignored congressional resolutions directing him to withdraw US forces from hostilities. If a Democrat-controlled Congress passes legislation restricting military operations or cutting funding for them, Trump can veto it.

Overriding a veto requires a two-thirds majority in both chambers, which Democrats are almost certain to fall short of.

On trade and tariffs, too, analysts see little room for Congress to rein in Trump.

The US president rattled global markets last year when he imposed “reciprocal” tariffs of 10 percent to 50 percent on some 90 countries, with the aim of shrinking the US trade deficit. The Asia Pacific was again hit harder than most. Some 15 countries were hit with tariffs, with Cambodia facing a 49 percent tariff and Laos 48 percent. Vietnam was slapped with 46 percent and Myanmar 45 percent.

After the Supreme Court struck down those tariffs in February, the Trump administration turned to other tools . In July, it imposed tariffs of 10 percent and 12.5 percent on goods from 60 trading partners, accusing them of failing to stop imports made with forced labour . In Asia, the list includes China, Japan, South Korea and seven Southeast Asian nations – Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.

“In some ways, the new Congress is not going to matter to the Asia Pacific because it’s not going to affect trade policy,” Okun said. “Congress cannot change that … Tariffs don’t change. The war doesn’t change.”

Still, some analysts see a narrow opening on tariffs.

Stephen Olson, a visiting fellow at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, argued in a recent essay that a “strong rebuke of ‘Trumpism’” at the polls could embolden a pro-free-trade wing of the Republican Party that has been “intimidated into standing down during the Trump presidency”.

That, Olson wrote, offers “a glimmer of hope” for Southeast Asian countries that depend on the US market. A Democratic-controlled Congress, he said, could also push for carve-outs and exceptions that would give the region’s exporters “a modicum of relief”. But any deeper shift in US trade policy, he added, will have to wait for the 2028 presidential election.

Joshua Kurlantzick, a senior fellow for Southeast Asia and South Asia at the Council on Foreign Relations, said the region’s wish list goes beyond trade to security.

“I think nearly all of Asia would like to see enormous changes, across many domains, during the rest of Trump’s term,” he told Al Jazeera. “But I think much of the region believes this will not happen.”

Besides “more stability” in trade and tariff policy, Asia-Pacific countries “would like to feel more stable in security guarantees from the US,” he said. They would also like a “more clear, obvious US presence” in the South China Sea , where China’s claims overlap with those of five Southeast Asian nations, and in the Taiwan Strait , which separates China from Taiwan , the self-governed island Beijing claims as its territory.

Businesses will also be watching whether a major Republican loss leads to “greater GOP willingness in Congress to stand up to Trump, along with Democrats, on issues important to companies in Asia,” Kurlantzick said, including tariffs, trade policy, arms sales and “overall economic unpredictability”.

One area where analysts do expect Congress to act is on China.

The new Congress, whichever party controls it, will pass tougher restrictions on China’s access to technology, said Okun at APAC Advisors.

These include the Remote Access Security Act, which would extend export controls to remote access of US goods, software or technology and the Chip Security Act, which would require companies to verify that advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips remain in authorised locations, to prevent diversion to foreign adversaries. It also includes the Multilateral Alignment of Technology Controls on Hardware Act, known as the MATCH Act, which would press allies to bring their controls on chipmaking equipment in line with Washington’s, to keep advanced chipmaking technology out of China’s hands.

“The next Congress is going to pass them regardless of midterms because both parties agree on them,” Okun said. “The person who is least restrictive now on China is the US president,” he added, referring to Trump’s courting of China’s President Xi Jinping.

The two men have met twice this year as ties have warmed after a bitter and costly trade war last year. To preserve the fragile trade truce, Trump has also held off approving a $14bn package of arms sales to Taiwan, which would be the largest ever for Taipei.

Some analysts meanwhile worry that a lame-duck Trump, hemmed in at home by a Democratic Congress, could turn more forcefully to foreign policy.

“We should not be surprised by continued erratic foreign policy,” said James Guild, an assistant professor at the Indonesian International Islamic University.

“The Democrats have a poor record of effectively opposing and holding Trump accountable using conventional tools of congressional oversight,” Guild said. “We will have to wait and see if they rise to the moment this time.”

articles.body:
The nonpartisan political handicapper Cook Political Report has shifted its rating of the 2026 Michigan Senate race to lean Democratic.

In a post Monday on the social platform X , the Cook Political Report said it was “issuing its final Senate ratings of the 2026 midterm cycle” and that “the Michigan Senate race moves from Toss Up to Lean Democrat.”

Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) made a last-minute endorsement of former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers (Mich.) on Sunday in his race against Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who defeated Stevens in the primary. The shake-up rattled Democrats but also pulled in $1.2 million for El-Sayed’s campaign .

Michigan is a key swing state that President Trump won two years ago and in 2016, while former President Biden won it in 2020. However, the electoral environment in this year’s midterms has challenged Republicans, with issues like Trump’s sagging approval rating, the unpopular war in Iran and concerns about the cost of living weighing the GOP down.

That same electoral environment may also have given El-Sayed a boost, with a recent New York Times/Siena University poll finding him ahead of Rogers by 11 points.

Decision Desk HQ rates the Michigan Senate race as likely Democratic , giving El-Sayed a 75 percent probability of earning a spot in the upper chamber.

In a Monday analysis , the Cook Political Report’s Jessica Taylor wrote that the handicapper was “basing our final ratings change on new public and private polling, including a New York Times/Siena poll over the weekend that put the race at an 11-point spread for El-Sayed.”

“Operatives on both sides don’t expect the race to be a double-digit blowout, but the Times survey notably also showed that El-Sayed has shored up his weakness with Black voters, which could have otherwise been his undoing,” she added.

articles.title: El-Sayed wants to pass ‘S‑‑‑ Lettuce Elimination Act’
articles.summary: Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D) told reporters that if he was elected to the upper chamber, he wanted to pass an act related to 2026’s cyclospora outbreak: The S‑‑‑ Lettuce Elimination Act. “For a long time here in Michigan, right, over the summer, there were a lot of people who ate lettuce and then…
articles.body:
Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D) told reporters that if he was elected to the upper chamber, he wanted to pass an act related to 2026’s cyclospora outbreak: The S‑‑‑ Lettuce Elimination Act.

“For a long time here in Michigan, right, over the summer, there were a lot of people who ate lettuce and then had, you know, they ate the s‑‑‑ lettuce. And we shouldn’t have s‑‑‑ lettuce in the United States of America,” he said Sunday.

The act is an ongoing joke from the Democrat who previously mentioned it during a campaign event in September but is related to his campaign’s public health priorities.

“We have to rebuild the part of the FDA [Food and Drug Administration] that makes sure that people are eating lettuce where other people have not shat,” El-Sayed continued. “And we need to make sure that the CDC [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention] can count the number of cases of s‑‑‑ lettuce. It’s a clean bill.”

El-Sayed was referring to one of the country’s largest outbreaks of cyclospora in history. It saw more than 12,000 reported cases in the U.S. with 570 hospitalizations, per the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). It was eventually linked to iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms de Mexico that has since been recalled.

The foodborne illness causes watery diarrhea “with frequent and sometimes explosive bowel movements,” according to the CDC.

More than 5,000 cases and the outbreak’s two deaths were recorded in Michigan . Health officials reported an end to the outbreak in September, which marked the country’s largest outbreak of cyclospora.

At the Monday press conference, El-Sayed said his first priority in the Senate was to block cuts to Medicaid. He is also advocating for “Medicare for all,” a topic he authored a book on.

The Democrat faces off against former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) in a battleground Senate election that could decide the majority in the upper chamber.

articles.title: Senado deve votar nesta terça PEC da Segurança Pública | G1
articles.standfirst: Governo mantém posição de não querer votar redução da maioridade penal junto com a PEC. Para ser aprovada, proposta precisa do apoio de 49 senadores em dois turnos de votação.
articles.summary: Governo mantém posição de não querer votar redução da maioridade penal junto com a PEC. Para ser aprovada, proposta precisa do apoio de 49 senadores em dois turnos de votação.
articles.body:
O plenário do Senado Federal deve votar nesta terça-feira (3) a proposta de emenda à Constituição (PEC) da Segurança Pública. O tema é considerado prioritário para o governo do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), que pretende, após a aprovação, criar o Ministério da Segurança Pública.

🔎 Para ser aprovada, uma PEC precisa ter ao menos três quintos dos votos favoráveis em dois turnos de votação. Ou seja, precisa contar com o apoio de 49 senadores .

A proposta estava prevista para ser analisada pelos senadores antes do segundo turno das eleições, mas um impasse sobre emendas que preveem a redução da maioridade penal levou o presidente do Senado, Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), a adiar a votação .

Líder do Governo no Senado, a senadora Teresa Leitão (PT-PE) afirmou que a posição do governo continua sendo não votar a maioridade penal junto com a PEC da Segurança . Ela lembra que o tema atualmente é discutido na Comissão Especial da Câmara.

"A redução da maioridade penal não é objeto da PEC da Segurança. Considera-se o chamado 'jabuti'. É um tema que precisa ser enfrentado com profundidade e ouvindo amplos setores da sociedade".

No entanto, a senadora aposta que o tema vai a voto e terão que disputar no plenário, sem acordo por parte deles.

O governo considera que o melhor caminho para aprovar a PEC é separar a discussão sobre a redução da maioridade penal e que não vai deixar de discutir a medida na hora certa.

Segundo o ministro das Relações Institucionais, José Guimarães, haverá uma reunião com os líderes do governo na manhã desta terça. Além disso, o presidente do Senado deve se reunir com os líderes antes da votação.

A dez dias do segundo turno das eleições presidenciais — onde Lula acabou vencendo o senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) — a oposição apresentou uma emenda para diminuir a maioridade penal para até 14 anos , a depender da gravidade do delito.

Como reação, o líder do PT no Senado, Camilo Santana (CE), apresentou uma alteração para reduzir para 16 anos em casos de crimes hediondos.

Aliados de Alcolumbre afirmaram que a retirada de pauta ocorreu porque nem o governo nem a oposição teriam votos suficientes para aprovar suas as emendas – e o cálculo, neste caso, seria de deixar o assunto para depois.

Apesar da ideia de Camilo neutralizar a proposta da oposição, a emenda apresentada dividiu a bancada do PT. Historicamente, a bancada do PT no Congresso Nacional se posicionou contra a redução da maioridade penal.

Diante da divisão na bancada governista e da proposta da oposição, o presidente do Senado retirou o tema da pauta com o argumento de que nem o governo e nem a oposição teriam votos suficientes para aprovar suas as emendas.

Plenário do Senado Federal — Foto: Jonas Pereira/Agência Senado

A PEC foi aprovada pela Comissão de Constituição e Justiça (CCJ) no dia 14 de outubro , antes do segundo turno das eleições. No mesmo dia, o Plenário aprovou um requerimento que permite acelerar a tramitação da matéria.

A medida dispensa as cinco sessões de discussão exigidas para a votação da proposta em primeiro turno e outras três necessárias para o segundo turno.

No mesmo dia em que a PEC saiu da pauta do Senado em meio ao racha na bancada governista do Senado, o presidente Lula se posicionou a favor da emenda de Camilo Santana ao ser questionado sobre o tema na sabatina da TV Globo .

"O meu pensamento, enquanto cidadão brasileiro, todo e qualquer crime hediondo, eu sou favorável a diminuir a pena. Para crimes hediondos. Eu sou a favor, sou a favor", afirmou o presidente.

Apesar do posicionamento favorável a mudança sugerida por Camilo, Lula defendeu que esse tema não fosse tratado na PEC da Segurança.

"Primeiro você discute a PEC, aprova a PEC e aí você pode discutir a maioridade penal ou não", disse.

Essa posição também é defendida por governistas, como a líder do governo no Senado, Teresa Leitão (PT-PE).

Caso algum trecho sobre maioridade seja aprovado e o texto precise voltar para a Câmara para aprovação dos deputados, governistas falam em "fatiar" a PEC .

Nesse cenário, a parte que já foi aprovada por deputados e senadores segue para promulgação, enquanto as partes que precisam de análise dos deputados, como a redução da maioridade penal, é enviada à Câmara como um texto separado.

➡️ A proposta estabelece na Constituição o Sistema Único de Segurança Pública (SUSP), com o objetivo de integrar a atuação das forças de segurança no combate ao crime organizado.

De acordo com o texto, União, estados e Distrito Federal poderão criar leis na área de segurança pública, incluindo forças-tarefa intergovernamentais, a organização das polícias e guardas municipais e o sistema socioeducativo .

➡️ Outro ponto central da PEC da Segurança Pública é o combate a crimes violentos e facções criminosas :

Entre as medidas está a obrigatoriedade de prisão em estabelecimento penal de segurança máxima ou de natureza especial .

Também ficam proibidas ou restringidas a progressão de regime, a concessão de liberdade provisória, com ou sem fiança, e de saída temporária .

➡️ A PEC também permite a expropriação de todo e qualquer bem, direito ou valor econômico envolvidos com as atividades criminosas. As regras valem para organizações criminosas, paramilitares e de milícia privada.

➡️ criação de polícias municipais para o policiamento ostensivo e comunitário;

➡️ ampliação da atuação da Polícia Rodoviária Federal (PRF) para o policiamento de hidrovias e ferrovias, além de apoiar outras forças de segurança, quando requisitada pelo governador;

➡️ manter Polícia Federal e PRF sob competência privativa da União, assim como as normas para atividades de inteligência.

Nesta terça-feira (3), os eleitores americanos vão às urnas para votar nas midterms, ou seja, nas eleições realizadas quando o mandato presidencial está pela metade. Esta votação é vista como uma espécie de referendo da população sobre o desempenho do presidente: quanto melhor sua avaliação, maior a chance de construir maioria no Congresso e de eleger seus aliados nos estados. Estão em jogo todas as 435 cadeiras da Câmara, 35 das 100 vagas do Senado e 36 governos estaduais. Hoje, o partido Republicano, de Donald Trump , controla as duas casas com maioria apertada. Mas as pesquisas de opinião apontam que o presidente americano está em seus níveis mais baixos de aprovação e indicam que o partido Democrata pode impor uma derrota dupla a Trump.

Neste episódio, Victor Boyadjian recebe dois convidados. Ele conversa com o jornalista Guga Chacra, que analisa, diretamente de Nova York, o mapa eleitoral americano e a influência da política externa de Trump para o humor do eleitor. Victor entrevista também o historiador Filipe Figueiredo, que analisa todos os cenários possíveis para o Congresso americano e suas consequências para o mundo.

articles.body:
Billionaire tax divides California Democrats, draws myriad questions

California voters this midterm cycle will decide whether the state will i mpose a wealth tax on billionaire residents, as wealthy Californians organize against the measure and experts say its potential broader impact on the state’s economy is nuanced.

By voting “yes” on Proposition 40 , Californians would support a one-time 5 percent tax on billionaires’ wealth.

The government revenue from the wealth tax — which no state to date has imposed — would primarily go toward state healthcare programs, with the remainder earmarked for food assistance and education initiatives.

The Golden State would collect “tens of billions of dollars” from the wealth tax on the roughly 200 billionaires in the state, per an analysis from the nonpartisan state Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO), which noted the increase in revenue would be “ spread across several years .”

But polling indicates it is unclear the measure will receive the simple majority support needed to pass. Even if it does, questions remain about next steps for the state and downstream effects.

“When you see eye-popping numbers like that, I can see how that looks … very appealing,” Tracy Gordon, the director of the Urban-Brookings Tax Policy Center, told The Hill. “But I think the concern is … what would the response be, both legally and economically, in terms of people leaving the state?”

The revenue from the tax, the group argues, could offset cuts to California’s federal funding under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act , which President Trump signed into law in July 2025.

The law could result in the state losing $30 billion in federal funding annually through 2028, per an analysis from the California State Assembly’s Committee on Health.

The measure, however, has not quite unified Democrats in the state. While the state Democratic Party along with the AFL-CIO and Teamsters unions support Proposition 40, California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) is against it.

Newsom, a potential 2028 presidential contender, wrote in a June Substack post that he supports a federal billionaire tax. But the outgoing California governor noted the state ballot measure “dedicates almost all of the revenue” from the tax to healthcare.
