articles.title: How a midterm tie gets settled in the case of the Senate
articles.summary: A tied Senate could leave control of the chamber uncertain after the 2026 midterm elections. Past 50-50 splits in 2000 and 2020 offer clues about how lawmakers could negotiate power sharing agreements in 2027.
articles.body: In the World Cup, they play overtime, then rely on penalty kicks to settle ties. The National Hockey League plays a short overtime, followed by a shootout. NHL games used to end in ties. In the playoffs, the teams keep going – until there’s a winner. In the 2020 playoffs, the Tampa Bay Lightning finally topped the Columbus Blue Jackets 3-2 after a staggering five overtimes. In other words. They played nearly THREE total games. That’s the equivalent of 26 innings in baseball. Speaking of Major League Baseball, teams play extra innings. And keep playing until one team is ahead and the home team has completed an at-bat in the bottom of the inning. MLB modified its rules a few years ago, introducing a "ghost runner" on second base to start the 10th inning. That’s an effort to end the tie and finish the game sooner. If only there were a method to settle a tie in the U.S. Senate. THE NINE KEY RACES THAT WILL DECIDE WHO CONTROLS THE SENATE, AND WHERE THEY STAND Yes. In the case of a tie roll call vote, the vice president — who doubles as president of the Senate – can vote to break a tie vote. In fact, the VP doesn’t even have to cast a ballot if it’s a tie and the roll call vote is going the way he or she wants. By rule, tie votes go down to defeat in the Senate. But what if we wake up Wednesday morning (if not Friday or Saturday morning or sometime in early December, depending on how hotly contested things are) to discover that the Senate is tied at 50-50? There is nothing in the Senate’s 44 standing rules which serves as a tiebreaker. The Founders didn’t provide a system to bust up a tie and determine which side is in the majority or minority. And no, it’s not written down anywhere that the party of the President is automatically thrust into the majority. Maybe soccer is on to something with penalty kicks. At least there’s a system. There’s nothing concrete to sort out which party controls the Senate if things are deadlocked at 50-50. There was a tie was a Senate tie in 1881 after resignations and political maneuvering. The Senate was also tied for a period in 1954. Nearly ten percent of all senators died during the two-year Congress which stretched from early 1953 to early 1955. However, the Senate featured two ties in recent Senate history. Both instances reflect what the Senate did to sort out which party captured the majority. One tie came after the 2000 election. The other in 2020. Both elections took a while to sort things out. In 2026, Alaska, we’re looking at you. It took until early December, 2000 to determine that Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., defeated then-Sen. Slade Gorton, R-Wash., establishing a 50-50 Senate. In fact, the tie for the Senate from the 2020 election wasn’t even established until two days into the new Congress on January 6, 2021. Yes. That was the day of the Capitol riot. Sens. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., and Raphael Warnock, D-Ga., both won runoffs to set the 50-50 split. In early December, 2000, the Supreme Court finally settled the Florida election dispute between President George W. Bush and Vice President Al Gore. Republicans had held the Senate. But then Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, R-Miss., and Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle, D-S.D., engineered a power-sharing agreement between the parties. This aligned with the election of Vice President Dick Cheney. Lott would serve as the Majority Leader and the GOP technically had the "majority." But the bipartisan pact granted Daschle some special floor powers. Republicans chaired each committee. However, there was equal representation by both parties on each panel. The full Senate had to ratify this agreement. And it did just that. Such a process is subject to two filibusters requiring 60 yeas. One to bring up the proposal for debate. Another to terminate the debate. Then a simple majority to pass it. But none of that was a problem. The Senate greenlighted it with all 100 senators signing on. Why such smooth sailing? Republicans feared Democrats would stall the agenda of President George W. Bush. So they got on board. Democrats agreed because they knew they were kinda, sorta in the majority. Otherwise, they were relegated to an outright minority. Former Senate Republican Leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., was well aware of those same dynamics in 2001. He insisted that Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., propound – word-for-word – the same accord in 2021 which Lott and Daschle hammered out. Which brings us to a potential tie in 2027. Is there the political will in the Senate – let alone the votes – to agree to such a compact? President Trump is still president. And Vice President JD Vance is still President of the Senate. What would they say about that? Unclear. The Senate isn’t compelled to present a dedicated "majority" or "minority." The concept of a "Majority Leader" is relatively new – only dating back to the early 20th Century. The Senate is a body of "equals." Thus, the Founders didn’t expect one senator to wield operational control of the Senate. You won’t find the words "Majority Leader" anywhere in the Constitution. Just Speaker of the House and President of the Senate. If there’s a 50-50 Senate and an impasse, could Vance suddenly have more power? Maybe. As President of the Senate, he can’t debate. He can only preside over the body and break ties. Moreover, would Vance even want to assert more authority? It’s unclear what that could be. And what would all of this do to his plans to run for president in 2028? EVERYTHING TO KNOW ABOUT HOUSE AND SENATE CONTROL, BALLOT MEASURES AND 2026 ELECTION DAY POLL CLOSING In fact, a deadlocked Senate with no power sharing agreement could potentially hamstring Vance. It wasn’t that long ago that the Vice President spent much of his time presiding over daily Senate debates. But not anymore. If there’s no set majority, those responsibilities either fall to Vance, current Senate President Pro Tempore Sen. Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, or the possible Democratic Senate President Pro Tempore Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash. The latter two are the most senior senators from their respective parties. The President Pro Tempore is third in line to the presidency, following the Vice President and House Speaker. A power sharing agreement is what helps determine who presides over the Senate. Otherwise, Vance may be moored in the Senate. So there is precedent for settling a "tie" in the Senate. But it hinges on the political will of senators. And if there are disputes about seating Members – say the Alaska Senate race or another contest becomes a conflagration – one can anticipate a toxic climate on Capitol Hill. Few may be willing to sign on to anything. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Senate relies a lot on history and precedent to do things. But absent political will, senators may just resort to rock, paper, scissors. Or maybe, penalty kicks.

articles.title: JD Vance says Haley Stevens' endorsement of GOP's Mike Rogers will 'certainly' help Michigan Senate race
articles.summary: VP JD Vance says Haley Stevens' endorsement of Mike Rogers over Abdul El-Sayed will give certain Michigan voters "permission" to back the GOP candidate.
articles.body: WASHINGTON, D.C. - Vice President JD Vance addressed Rep. MICHIGAN DEM CLAIMS STEVENS SHOT DOWN ROGERS ENDORSEMENT RUMOR HOURS BEFORE TURNING ON EL-SAYED "I do think it drives home the message, maybe gives certain voters who, you know, wouldn't normally vote for a Republican permission, knowing that the Democratic Congresswoman of Michigan is going to support Mike Rogers." EL SAYED'S LEFT-WING ALLIES ATTACK 'EVIL' STEVENS AFTER BOMBSHELL ROGERS ENDORSEMENT Stevens endorsed Rogers on Sunday, while taking a swipe at El-Sayed in the process. MAMDANI, HASAN PIKER AMONG RADICAL LEFT-WING VOICES ERUPTING OVER HALEY STEVENS' ENDORSEMENT SWITCH Both El-Sayed and Rogers penned opinion pieces for Fox News Digital on Monday ahead of Election Day, with the two candidates laying out their reasoning for entering the race. EL-SAYED, ROGERS CLASH OVER MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD, TRUMP AND GUNS: 5 FIERY DEBATE MOMENTS Rogers didn’t spare El-Sayed from criticism in his piece, noting his Democrat opponent's connection to far-left communist streamer and activist Hasan Piker. ABDUL EL-SAYED REPORTEDLY CALLED HASAN PIKER WARNING HIS RHETORIC WAS 'COSTING' VOTES Stevens also criticized El-Sayed’s connection to Piker following her endorsement of Rogers, and has previously said Piker "should be condemned" for his extremist views. The Party for Socialism and Liberation and ANSWER Coalition share office space at the People's Forum and share leadership with the People's Forum. After Vance returned to Joint Base Andrews in Washington, D.C., on Monday afternoon, El-Sayed and Rogers both held rallies in Michigan in a final message to voters. articles.title: Talarico says he wants to work with Trump on bipartisan MAGA agenda
articles.summary: Democratic Texas Senate candidate James Talarico said he would want to work with President Trump on a bipartisan “Make America Great Again” agenda. “I would love, as the next U.S. senator from Texas, to work with Donald Trump to actually fulfill some of the promises of his political project,” Talarico stated during an interview with…
articles.body:
Democratic Texas Senate candidate James Talarico said he would want to work with President Trump on a bipartisan “Make America Great Again” agenda.

“I would love, as the next U.S. senator from Texas, to work with Donald Trump to actually fulfill some of the promises of his political project,” Talarico stated during an interview with “ The Diary of a CEO .”

“Because the promise of MAGA was that we were going to transform this government so that it delivered for the people who have been left behind, the people who have been forgotten in this country, and there’s still time to do that,” he continued.

Talarico expressed that there was “still time to do that” in the last two years of Trump’s second term in the White House “on a bipartisan basis.”

“If the president wants to work with me or with any Democrat to expand healthcare access, I’m there,” the Democrat said, adding that he would similarly appear to “build millions of new homes” and “slash the red tape.”

“So my hope is that this midterm will be a wake up call for the president, for his administration, and as a result, they will reverse course,” he concluded. “They will decide to engage with leaders in both parties to actually deliver for the working people who sent him there.”

Talarico — a Texas state legislator — is racing against Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) in one of the most contested and watched Senate races in the country.

It would be a shock for the Democrat to win a state that Trump carried in all of his presidential bids, but Paxton has struggled to pull ahead in polling leading up to Election Day.

The possibility of flipping a seat in the red stronghold comes as Trump rallied in the state four times. He nicknamed Talarico “Democrat Communist James Talafreako.”

“Talafreako stated that he wants to dismantle Texas oil and gas and capitalism itself. He wants to take it apart,” Trump told supporters at one Texas rally, adding that Talarico will “kill millions of Texas jobs.”

A recent New York Times/Siena poll reported Talarico leading by 7 points over Paxton, with 6 percent saying they still didn’t know who to choose or refused to answer.

Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) shared her rationale for her recent decision to endorse former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) over Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in the state’s contested Senate race, citing campaign ads, among other reasons.

“Once I concluded that Abdul El-Sayed is not fit to serve in the United States Senate, I had to confront who should,” she wrote in a lengthy X article .

“Instead of asking why a lifelong Democrat reached this point, some leaders rushed to condemn me, question my motives, and push me out,” she said. “That response reveals something deeply troubling about what is missing in today’s Democratic Party.”

Stevens endorsed Rogers following an appearance at a Detroit church event on Sunday. The last-minute decision created a rift between the Democratic lawmaker and her party as the Michigan Democratic Party has already ousted her . She remains in the Congressional Democratic caucus for the upcoming lame duck session.

In the post, Stevens noted two campaign ads backing El-Sayed fueled her decision: “One, from a group supporting Abdul, tied the cost of groceries to America’s support for Israel. Another, from Abdul’s own campaign, featured Tucker Carlson.”

The lawmaker recalled a previous statement that asked El-Sayed to condemn the ad that tied rising grocery prices to U.S. military aid to Israel. She was “offering him an opportunity to reassure people, reject division, and demonstrate the leadership required of a United States Senator,” Stevens said in her Monday post.

Stevens added El-Sayed’s ties to political streamer Hasan Piker were “deeply disturbing” and “raised serious questions about his judgment and his ability to bring people together.”

She also disputed reports that her fiancé, Jason Turkish , influenced her decision to endorse Rogers.

“That is sexism dressed up as political analysis. My fiancé has his own views. I have mine. I made this decision, and I am proud of it. Do not question my independence simply because you disagree with my conclusion,” Stevens said.

Stevens concluded her statement by asserting that she “still believe[s] in the promise of the Democratic Party.”

“But fulfilling that promise will require something more than loyalty tests and demands for blind obedience,” she asserted. “We can build a stronger, more welcoming, more courageous Democratic Party. And I plan to help lead that effort.”

El-Sayed brushed off Stevens’s endorsement of Rogers on Sunday, telling reporters, “at the end of the day, I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens.”

He is “likely to win” against Rogers, according to Decision Desk HQ , The Hill’s partner. The Cook Political Report , a nonpartisan political handicapper, also shifted the race to “lean Democrat” in its final shift before Tuesday’s midterm election.

articles.title: US midterms present a test for Republican redistricting in Texas and beyond
articles.summary: Partisan redistricting has transformed elections for Black voters in Houston as Democrats seek new pathways to victory.
articles.body:
Houston, Texas – The gospel music from Mount Hebron Missionary Baptist Church spills into the streets of Sunnyside, a predominantly Black neighbourhood in southern Houston.

It is a familiar scene on any given Sunday: hands in the air, immaculate bow ties on starched shirts, fabric flowers adorning perfectly pastel hats. But with the US midterm elections just two days away, the service held a special significance on the front line of a US redistricting battle .

Mt Hebron had long been located in the ninth congressional district, its politically engaged Black voters for two decades helping to elect Democrat Al Green, a flamboyant presence in Congress known for his cane-waving opposition to US President Donald Trump.

But following an appeal from Trump, the Republican state legislature last year conducted rare mid-decade redistricting, redrawing the church and its Black community into the Black-majority 18th district.

Critics call the process “cracking and packing”, diminishing the representation in Congress of minority groups, particularly heavily Democratic Black communities, by consolidating their voting power into fewer districts.

“It’s kind of one and the same when we talk about the voting and the civil rights,” said Pastor Max Miller, who has served at the church for 18 years.

“They are trying to manipulate and monopolise the vote and minimise the people who are in those districts,” said Miller. “We see so much rolling backwards that it looks like they’re trying to take a script from an old song and turn back the hands of time.”

As a result of the redistricting, Green was forced to run in a primary against 18th district incumbent Christian Menefee, another Black Democrat. He lost, and Houston lost one of its Black representatives in Congress.

The ninth district, meanwhile, was redrawn to favour Republicans, one of at least five US congressional seats the party hopes to pick up in the midterm vote.

The machinations have resonated with worshippers at Mt Hebron.

“I don’t like the redistricting at all because Al Green was moved out,” said 97-year-old Alice Jefferson, who had followed the congressman throughout his political career. “He always had good advice for the people.”

Janice Ray, a 61-year-old home health aide and entrepreneur, said state lawmakers were “trying to move people out of the district that they’re familiar with”.

“To me, it was all a bunch of BS,” she said. “There was no reason for it.”

“But we’ll stand firm, regardless of what they try to do,” Ray added. “Because just like it was changed, it can always be changed back.”

The redistricting process has undergone a generational transformation this election season, one that, experts say, has degraded longstanding guardrails protecting minority voting power.

“In political science, we have what we call descriptive representation,” Michael Adams, a professor at Texas Southern University in Houston, told Al Jazeera. “In terms of descriptive representation, minorities and others feel that if they can elect someone who reflects their values, for example, and who may look like them, their voting can be defined as one voice.”

“And certainly with not having an additional Black member of Congress representing Houston, a significant segment of Black voters may feel that their voices have been weakened,” he said.

This year Republican and Democratic state legislatures across the country joined the spree: Republicans successfully redistricted in Missouri, North Carolina, Tennessee, Louisiana, Alabama, Florida and Ohio; Democrats did so in California, while a court-ordered map in Utah handed Democrats a favourable seat. A Democratic push in Virginia was subsequently invalidated.

Redrawing maps mid-decade, and not waiting for the latest demographic numbers from the US census, was already atypical. But many of the maps drawn this year would have been deemed illegal in previous cycles.

Section 2 of the landmark Voting Rights Act of 1965, initially passed to counter blatantly racist voting practices in the US, had long prohibited redrawing congressional maps to dilute the electoral power of minority voters.

In April, the conservative-dominated US Supreme Court ruled that anyone challenging such a map must prove “racist intent”. Critics have said the ruling effectively allows for racial gerrymandering, with proving such an intent an unreasonably high bar.

But critics of Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act have said drawing maps to protect minority voting power is in itself discriminatory.

Defenders in Texas, meanwhile, have said the redistricting was based on the shifting political makeup of the state, and not racial gerrymandering.

“This plan includes political considerations, public testimony, recognition of population growth and recent changes in voter trends,” State Representative Todd Hunter, a Republican, said shortly after the new map’s passage last year.

“Each of these newly drawn districts now trend Republican in political performance. While there’s no guarantee of electoral success, Republicans will now have an opportunity to potentially win these districts,” he said.

There are no guarantees that a party’s redistricting plans will actually work.

Following the tit-for-tat map redrawings, Republicans hoped to net at least 13 seats nationally. Polling has suggested their gains may be much more muted.

All told, about 35 million US voters will be casting ballots in newly redistricted seats this election.

“Redistricting can change the political boundaries, but it can’t guarantee how voters will behave,” Brandon Rottinghaus, a professor at the University of Houston, told Al Jazeera.

In Texas, the Republican map was drawn largely based on recent Latino voting trends. The demographic swung heavily for Trump in the state in 2024, despite once being considered a reliable Democratic voting bloc.

Beyond the ninth congressional district in Houston, Republicans hoped to pick up four other districts, most based in South Texas, with an eye on shifting Latino sentiment.

But the political tides have again turned. Trump’s popularity has tanked among Latino voters, fuelled in part by unrest over the economy and the administration’s aggressive deportation campaign.

It remains to be seen how that will reflect at the ballot box when Texas voters pick a senator, governor, members of Congress and a slate of state and local officials.

“These districts are a test of whether political dissatisfaction can overcome an aggressively partisan map,” Rottinghaus said.

With new boundaries come new opportunities.

The ninth district is now considered Republican-favoured, but its large population of low-propensity Latino voters creates a pathway for a Democratic victory, according to Dayana Iza, Texas state director of Mi Familia Vota, a Latino voting organisation that has focused resources on the congressional race.

The state legislature “kept a big portion of Latino voters there, but the reality is that the Latino percentage in that district that votes is very, very low,” Iza told Al Jazeera. “So that then became a district that we are trying to mobilise in terms of turnout.”

On the Saturday ahead of the November 3 vote, Democratic candidate Leticia Gutierrez and State Senator Molly Cook zigzagged through a neighbourhood of single-family homes in eastern Houston.

Any path to victory, Gutierrez assessed, would be based on face time and a chance to connect with disillusioned voters.

“This community here has an average annual income of $63,000 a year. I make a little over that, and it’s difficult,” Gutierrez told Al Jazeera. “At this point, it’s not a left or a right thing anymore. This is an affordability crisis.”

“You’ve heard some of the voters out here say this is the first time someone actually came to my door,” she added. “That means a lot, and so we want to continue to do that.”

Among the residents was Christian Garcia, a 53-year-old who works at a local chemical plant and has not voted since moving to Texas from Puerto Rico in 2014. He said he is focused on his family, saving enough for retirement and eventually leaving some money behind for his adult children.

In the past, Garcia said, he felt voting was “wasting my time”.

“You know, it’s a lot of corruption and things,” said Garcia. “I just don’t believe in anybody anymore.”

Down the block, Esmeralda Gil, a 39-year-old teacher, said she hoped for a Democratic surge.

Gil questioned why taxes, particularly on housing, seemed so high, while so many struggled to access healthcare.

“We need affordable healthcare and affordable housing,” she said.

articles.title: What time do polls open and close in the US midterm elections 2026?
articles.summary: The first polls are set to open in Vermont at 5am (10:00 GMT).
articles.body:
More than 230 million eligible voters across the United States can head to the polls on Tuesday to decide who will represent them in Congress.

All 435 House of Representatives seats and 35 of the Senate’s 100 seats are being contested . Voters in 36 states will also elect governors. Republicans currently hold both chambers.

Voting hours are determined and set by each state.

The first polls are set to open in Vermont at 5am (10:00 GMT). Voting in New Jersey, Virginia, Connecticut and Kentucky will start at 6am (11:00 GMT).

Voting in Georgia, Florida, Pennsylvania and New York will start between 6am (11:00 GMT) and 7am (12:00 GMT), while Ohio and North Carolina will see voting start at 6:30am (11:30 GMT).

In Michigan, polls will open at 7am (12:00 GMT).

Polls close in waves across the country, with the earliest closures at 6pm (23:00 GMT) in Indiana and Kentucky.

Voting in Michigan closes at 8pm and in Kansas at 7pm local time (both 01:00 GMT on Wednesday), while polls in Iowa close at 8pm (02:00 GMT on Wednesday).

Alaska is the last to close, at around 1am Eastern Time (06:00 GMT) on Wednesday.

The first results could start arriving on Tuesday as polls begin to close.

Results will continue to come in throughout Tuesday evening, and some on Wednesday as more states finish voting and officials start releasing their vote counts.

However, the first reported results will not necessarily mean that a winner has been announced.

Election officials release vote counts as ballots are processed, while news organisations such as the Associated Press analyse the results and determine when a race can be called.

Closely contested races could take hours, or even days, to call. It might not be immediately clear which party will control Congress.

How does the American voting system work in the midterms?

Voters can cast their ballots by mail, early or in person on election day, which is Tuesday.

Many mail, provisional and other ballots are counted after election night, which is why tallies can take a few days, or even weeks, to finalise.

Senate Democrats need a net gain of four seats to reach a majority. House Democrats need three seats for a majority.

Here are a few key races to watch as the two parties go head-to-head:

In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers are locked in a closely watched race after Democratic Representative Haley Stevens decided to endorse Rogers on Sunday.

In Florida, Democrat Angie Nixon is challenging Republican Senator Ashley Moody.

In Georgia, Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff will face Republican Mike Collins.

In Maine, Republican Senator Susan Collins is up against Democrat Troy Jackson.

In New Hampshire, Democratic Representative Chris Pappas is on the ballot against Republican John Sununu, a former senator.

In North Carolina, Democrat Roy Cooper and Republican Michael Whatley are on the ballot.

articles.title: Americans vote in midterms that could define Trump's closing chapter
articles.summary: The midterms will shape Congress for the last years of his presidency, writes Sarah Smith, but they are also a test of what politics may look like without him.
articles.body:
With two years of his presidency remaining, Donald Trump, who has dominated American politics over the past decade and transformed it in remarkable ways, is facing potentially pivotal elections.

And the midterm elections on Tuesday that will decide control of Congress come at a difficult moment for his Republican Party.

Voters overwhelmingly say they are most concerned about the cost of living. Food and fuel prices have soared in part due to the president's aggressive tariffs and unpopular war with Iran, so it will be top of mind as many head to the polls.

Trump, who has faced record low approval ratings in recent months, has been campaigning hard, headlining dozens of rallies across the country.

But high prices are a concern for voters on all sides - which helps explain why he has been campaigning in previously safe Republican territory, appearing in Iowa and Kansas during a final weekend blitz.

His party has also poured hundreds of millions of dollars of campaign advertising into these traditionally safe contests, such as the Senate race in Kansas.

"When they start spending hard American dollars on political advertising in a state that they should be winning, that's how you know that they think they're in trouble," Carrie Dann, the managing editor of the Cook Political Report, which analyses campaigns and elections, told the BBC.

"The spending [in Kansas] is going to be far more than Republicans ever anticipated," she added. That points to a party that is approaching these elections on the defensive.

At many of his rallies, Trump has also made a plea to voters. "In this election, I'm asking you to pretend, please, that I'm on the ballot," he said last month. "Just pretend."

Of course, he is not on the ballot. But this plea - which he made again in Iowa on Sunday - gets to the heart of a critical question: Is he still an electoral asset for his Republican Party?

The answer to that is not as simple as it once was.

Trump returned to the White House as a formidable force following his crushing 2024 election win - and had the healthy approval ratings to match. Before that, during the previous midterm elections in 2022, his endorsement was courted by Republicans who saw it as vital to success.

Now, with the war with Iran dragging on and hitting many Americans in the pocket, his approval ratings have sunk. The price of a gallon of diesel - which was $3.75 before the war started in February - hit a record high of $6.52 in September.

"I literally just had my son drive across the country, and he called me in every state and told me the price of gas," one voter in Iowa told me. "And I was like - 'oh my gosh, this is horrible'."

Inflation has also ticked up from 3% when Trump took office to 3.7% today, and economists estimate it would have been lower without his sweeping regime of global tariffs.

There is concern among Republicans that this economic picture has left them vulnerable in typically safe races, in states such as Texas, Ohio and Kansas.

"The southern states, the midwestern states, the American heartland - that is where Republicans tend to thrive," said Stephen Hawkins, the global director of research at the pollster More in Common.

"But that is where the Senate races that are so interesting are playing out right now."

"Places where President Trump won by 10, 12, 15 points just two years ago in the presidential race are now states where Democrats have a very viable chance of taking a Senate seat," he said.

When I asked voters in Iowa, a state Trump won in 2024 that has been hit by soaring fuel and fertiliser costs, whether the president would make people more or less likely to back Republicans - the answer was revealing.

"With the current climate, I would think possibly less, believe it or not," Paul Ross told me outside a busy college football game. "As a Republican myself, I would think it might be detrimental."

"I think it definitely puts voters off, there's no doubt about that, and I do think it probably raises the Democratic side to a level that isn't always there, just because it's Donald Trump," added Zach Shimp.

"He's got us in the war," another voter, Rose Heming, said. "Prices and groceries [are] high - sky high - gas is sky high."

That is the story of this election. Many voters, including in solidly Republican states, are hurting financially and polls suggest they may want to make this known at the ballot box on Tuesday.

But it is too simplistic to think this backdrop of war, tariffs and soaring prices will usher in a thumping Democratic victory in the House, Senate and governors' races.

Many Republican voters are angry with the president, but not so angry that they would vote for a Democrat. It is a mistake to assume that Trump's weak approval ratings translate to increasing popularity for the other side.

In fact, final polls taken before the elections suggest Trump's approval rating is around 38%. That is low - but the same polls, including a national NBC poll released on Sunday , indicate that only 29% of voters view the Democratic Party positively.

Voter frustration is no guarantee of a willingness to switch sides on Tuesday.

"We like to stay out of people's business," Tim McKinnon, a Republican in Iowa who voted for Trump in 2024 told me last month. "And so [Trump's] world stage interventions time after time after time - we don't love it.

"We didn't expect him to necessarily be a perfect choir boy obviously," his wife, Michelle, added. "We voted for the underbelly of what he was standing for."

The Democratic Party cannot rely on voters like the McKinnons, who are frustrated with elements of Trump's recent agenda, to back them. They do not think Democrats will ever reflect their Christian, conservative values.

"One dollar more on gas is not going to change what we believe in," Tim McKinnon told me.

If Democrats do win a large swathe of seats on Tuesday night, it won't necessarily be because voters love them – they just hate them a little less.

The party, however, is already looking ahead to a 2028 presidential election in which they will have to unite behind a single candidate. That is easier said than done given their clear fractures - some of which spilled out publicly during this election cycle, including in Michigan over the weekend.

Democrats will be closely watching these results for lessons ahead of 2028. Can they really win in Texas? Can they tempt rural voters in deep Republican strongholds? And will some of their rising stars, such as Jon Ossoff in Georgia and James Talarico in Texas, live up to the hype?

If the answer to some of these questions is no, there will be much to ponder for the party over the next year. And the post-mortem may not be pretty.

"This represents an opportunity, really, for Democrats to expand a lot of their influence, not just in terms of numbers, but in terms of perception of where they can compete," Hawkins, from the pollster More in Common, said.

Republican attempts, including from Trump himself, to paint the Democrats as dangerous communists have not landed with all voters.

In Detroit, Michigan, Nicole Williams - who owns her own hairdressing salon - summed up the view of many people I spoke to. "Anything is better than what we have now," she said. "Socialist? Socialised? It don't matter to me. Lower my cost of living."

"People are just tired of the disrespect to Americans, because he is an American," Gwen Jackson, another Michigan voter, said, referring to the state's left-wing Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed who Trump has repeatedly attacked.

"People are just tired," she said. "They're ready to see a change."

Even when a sitting president is more popular than Trump, their party usually loses seats in the midterms. This, combined with the latest polling, means there is confidence among Democrats that they will at least win the House of Representatives.

"It's the cost of living, it's the undeclared war," Democratic strategist Mary Anne Marsh said of the key issues. "Every Republican who did not stand up to Donald Trump is about to realise the consequences of believing he was invincible."

If the Democrats do win the House, the party could try to block any legislation Trump wants to pass. That is unlikely to worry him, given he has already tried to bypass Congress as much as possible and rule by signing executive orders from the Oval Office instead.

Trump will be more concerned about the investigations Democrats will be able to launch if they take control of the House. They may also try to impeach some of his cabinet members, with Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth seen as a likely candidate due to the war in Iran.

Winning the Senate on Tuesday is likely to be a much harder task for Democrats.

Thirty-five seats are up for election, and they will need a net gain of four to win control. If they lose in Michigan - a battleground seat they already hold - they will need a net gain of five seats to win it.

Most of the battleground races are close and several sit within the margin of error for pollsters. The crucial Senate races to watch are in Michigan, Texas, Ohio, Iowa, Maine, Alaska and North Carolina.

This is, in reality, where these midterm elections will be won and lost.

There is, as always with American elections, an important caveat around the polls. They have historically overestimated the Democratic Party and underestimated President Trump, who appears convinced that he can once again defy them.

But if the polls are close to correct about the suggested surge of support for Democrats, then he could be looking at painful defeats in states that have been reliable Republican strongholds for decades.

How Trump may respond to any stinging losses is an open question. He has repeatedly questioned the integrity and security of these elections , and the possibility that he does so again as votes are still being counted or when results are declared is a very real one.

These elections, however, represent a hugely significant moment for Americans, many of whom want to see real change over the next two years.

For both parties, they will serve as the final electoral test before a 2028 presidential election that will determine what a post-Trump politics looks and feels like. And for the president himself, they are an opportunity for voters to cast judgement on how he and his party are performing.

As Trump looks to shape his legacy in the next two years, the question is whether a change in control of Congress, which he has largely bypassed, would really curb his presidency at all.

articles.title: Mamdani threatens to sue Trump admin over ICE's use of city-owned lots for immigration enforcement
articles.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani threatened legal action against ICE over agents allegedly staging immigration enforcement operations in city-owned parking lots.
articles.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a Democrat, threatened to sue the Trump administration over Immigration and Customs Enforcement's (ICE) reported use of city-owned parking lots to stage immigration enforcement operations without the city's authorization. In a letter addressed to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, acting ICE Director David Venturella and ICE New York field office Director Kenneth Genalo, Mamdani said he is "deeply troubled" by reports of ICE agents "using property owned by the City of New York to stage enforcement operations," which the mayor said is unauthorized and illegal. "This use of City property in furtherance of federal immigration enforcement is unauthorized and is therefore illegal, endangers City residents, and sows fear among those who seek to access City property," Mamdani wrote in the letter. "If your agents continue any unauthorized use of these lots, New York City will take legal action to prevent this unlawful commandeering of City property." DEMOCRAT MAYOR BLASTED BY DHS FOR 'HUNTING DOWN' PROPERTY OWNERS LEASING TO ICE: 'UNHINGED' According to the mayor's letter, ICE agents have reportedly parked their vehicles and conducted meetings in several city-owned, unstaffed parking lots, including in a parking lot at Van Cortlandt Park in the Bronx as well as in parking lots along 111th Street on the west side of Flushing Meadows Corona Park in Queens, which is located next to a city-run preschool and several cultural institutions welcome hundreds of children and families every day. "ICE has not secured any authorization from the City to use these lots for immigration enforcement. To be clear: the City does not authorize ICE using its property in this manner," Mamdani wrote. "Parking lots connected to City parks are reserved for the safe use and enjoyment of New Yorkers and visitors who wish to use our parks," he continued. "Use of these lots for other purposes, including ICE’s reported use of these lots, amounts to unauthorized activity on City property. Accordingly, you must immediately issue guidance to your agents prohibiting them from using any City lots to stage or conduct enforcement operations." Mamdani added that New York City "deeply values its immigrant communities and will continue to use all available lawful means to ensure their safety, well-being, and ability to navigate the City and its resources without fear." articles.body:
Election Day has arrived and Democrats are now projected to take control of the Senate if voters behave as polls predict.

Polls show a blue wave is forming that could flip as many as eight Senate seats from Republican to Democratic control.

President Trump’s sliding job approval rating and voter anger over rising prices, the war with Iran and the rise of AI-driven data centers have created major political headwinds for GOP candidates.

Yet Senate Republicans and allied outside-money groups have vastly outspent their Democratic counterparts and many of the battleground states historically have been favorable ground for Republicans.

Democrats also have had to worry about internal party divisions in Michigan and the fallout from a public corruption scandal in Minnesota that may give Republicans a chance to steal two Democratic-held seats.

Many of the key races are within the polls’ margins of error. This has Republicans hopeful they will keep their Senate majority despite indications that Democrats have the momentum heading into election night.

Here are the 10 Senate seats most likely to flip:

Everything has gone right for Democrats in the Tar Heel State.

Democrats got their top-recruit candidate — North Carolina’s former Gov. Roy Cooper (D) — and the state’s savvy two-term Republican senator, Thom Tillis, suddenly announced his retirement in June of last year after clashing with Trump over big cuts to Medicaid.

GOP candidate Michael Whatley, who is also the former chair of the North Carolina Republican Party, has had to struggle with having a much lower name ID across the state than his Democratic opponent.

It became clear over the summer that the race was slipping away from the GOP and Senate Republican super PACs canceled millions of dollars in television ad reservations in September.

Trump won North Carolina by slightly more than 3 percentage points in 2024. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates North Carolina as a “likely” Democratic win.

Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) scored another impressive recruiting win in Ohio by persuading former three-term Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio), who was once considered a promising presidential or vice presidential candidate, to run for the seat.

Brown — who narrowly lost his reelection race to Sen. Bernie Moreno (R) in 2024, a year when Trump carried Ohio by 11.2 percentage points — is viewed as the favorite over incumbent Republican Sen. Jon Husted.

Brown and his Democratic allies spent heavily on ads attacking Husted’s past support for data centers, which spurred the incumbent senator to become the lead sponsor of the Ratepayer Protection Act, which would prod states to come up with laws to protect taxpayers from data center-associated costs.

Brown leads Husted by an average of 2 percentage points, according to a compilation of recent polls by Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Democrats cheered when former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) decided to challenge low-profile Sen. Dan Sullivan (R), as the party saw Peltola as representing their best chance to knock off a two-term incumbent in a GOP-leaning state.

Peltola has shown she can win statewide in Alaska. She was elected to succeed longtime GOP Rep. Don Young after he died in 2022.

She beat former Alaska Gov. Sarah Palin (R) in that year’s runoff special election and then won a full term in the 2022 general election.

Sullivan has been battered by the impact of high gas and diesel prices on Alaska’s residents, who pay more per capita for diesel and home heating oil than voters in any other state.

Democrats have bashed Sullivan for rising health insurance costs due to the expiration of enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies and Alaskans losing coverage because of Medicaid reforms Republicans enacted last year.

Peltola leads Sullivan by about a percentage point and a half, according to an average of recent polls compiled by DDHQ.

The race was thrown into turmoil last week after The New York Times published an investigative report alleging that Peltola’s campaign was aware of the work by a Democratic operative who recruited little-known candidate Daniel J. Sullivan to run for Senate in a bid to siphon away votes from the Republican incumbent with the same name.

Peltola has denied any involvement in the dirty-tricks campaign.

Trump lost Maine to Democrats Hillary Clinton, Joe Biden and Kamala Harris in the last three presidential elections, which should make veteran GOP Sen. Susan Collins’s seat a likely pickup opportunity for Democrats.

But Collins has shown throughout her 30-year Senate career that she knows how to win tough races and how to defy the polls.

Surveys showed Democratic Senate candidate Sara Gideon comfortably ahead of Collins in the final weeks of the 2020 election, but Collins wound up winning by nearly 10 percentage points.

Maine Democrats were rocked when progressive candidate Graham Platner dropped out of the race in July due to sexual assault allegations, but the party quickly coalesced behind Troy Jackson (D), who previously served as president of the Maine state Senate.

Collins has worked diligently to distance herself from Trump on big issues. She voted against the president’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act and his most controversial Cabinet nominees.

She has touted her ability to deliver for Maine as chair of the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee and her ability to win exemptions for critical goods from Trump’s global tariff policies.

Jackson leads Collins by an average of nearly 6 percentage points, according to recent polls compiled by DDHQ. Even so, Collins has defied the polls before, and she is viewed as probably the best GOP Senate candidate in any of this year’s battleground races.

The Texas Senate race has been one of the most closely watched contests of the 2026 midterm elections because of nasty intraparty squabbling among Republicans and huge Democratic voter enthusiasm for progressive candidate James Talarico.

Democrats may be on the cusp of electing a candidate from Texas to the U.S. Senate for the first time since 1988 if the polls are accurate due to Republican divisions, a decisive shift of Hispanic voters toward Democrats and the state’s changing demographics.

Talarico’s lead over Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton is no big surprise to Senate GOP leaders who warned for months that Paxton would be a weak general election candidate.

Talarico leads Paxton by an average of 3.5 percentage points, according to recent polls compiled by DDHQ.

Wealthy GOP donors have poured massive amounts of cash into the race, spending an estimated $300 million to prop up Paxton.

Elon Musk, the world’s wealthiest person, has spent nearly $170 million alone to support Paxton, according to The Dallas Morning News.

Strategists on both sides say the race is extremely close in a state that Trump won by nearly 14 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election.

GOP Sen. Ted Cruz (Texas) warned on his podcast that early voting by Democrats has swamped that of Republicans and that Republicans could lose every statewide race in Texas.

“Texas is excruciatingly close. Understand we could lose Texas,” he warned. “Not just the Senate race. We could lose every single statewide race in Texas. That’s how close these numbers are.”

Michigan is a Democratic-leaning state that Trump narrowly won in the 2016 and 2020 presidential elections, but where Republican statewide candidates have struggled in recent years.

GOP candidate Mike Rogers’s recent internal polling showed him tied with Democrat Abdul El-Sayed. And Republicans have tried to stir up voters’ fears about electing the first Muslim to the U.S. Senate by warning of El-Sayed’s alleged links to the Muslim Brotherhood.

El-Sayed’s strong criticism of Israel and the support of pro-Palestinian advocates such as left-wing Twitch streamer Hasan Piker has made him a divisive figure, especially among centrist Jewish Democrats.

Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), who lost a tough-fought race to El-Sayed in the Democratic Senate primary, roiled the race by unexpectedly endorsing Rogers on Sunday.

But Stevens’s decision to back Rogers after she and El-Sayed clashed over campaign strategy may not have much of an impact coming so late in the race.

Schumer called Stevens’s endorsement a “despicable betrayal” and most other Democrats are unified behind El-Sayed, who is the favorite heading into the final day of the race.

El-Sayed leads Rogers by an average of 3.5 percentage points, according to DDHQ.

Democrats have a chance to win in Iowa because the state’s agriculture-reliant economy has been hit hard by Trump’s global trade policies, which have shrunk the export market for corn and soybeans — two major Iowa commodities.

Iowa farmers are also furious over the high price of diesel, which they blame on the eight-month war with Iran, setting up a perfect opportunity for Democrats to win a Senate seat in a state that Trump carried by 13.2 percentage points in 2024.

Former President Obama carried Iowa in the 2008 and 2012 presidential elections, and former liberal Sen. Tom Harkin (D) represented the state in the Senate for 30 years.

The Republican candidate, Rep. Ashley Hinson, is well-regarded among GOP aides and strategists, and she has scrambled to distance herself from the president amid voter anger over fuel and food prices.

Schumer’s allies were heartened when Democratic candidate Josh Turek, a two-time Paralympic gold medalist in basketball and a state legislator, emerged as the victor in the Democratic primary over more progressive Iowa state Sen. Zach Wahls (D).

Polls show the Hawkeye State’s Senate race is closer than the contests in North Carolina, Ohio, Maine, Texas and Michigan, where the Democratic candidates have bigger leads.

But agriculture plays a bigger role in Iowa’s economy than just about any other state, and farmers aren’t happy about being squeezed by low commodity prices and high fuel costs — giving Democrats a chance to win.

Kansas is another farm state that has been hit hard by the president’s trade wars and high fertilizer and diesel prices linked to the war with Iran.

Democrats haven’t elected a candidate from Kansas to the U.S. Senate since 1932, and Trump won the state by 16 points in 2024.

Yet Democrats have shown some signs of life in the Jayhawk State in recent years.

Democrat Laura Kelly has served as the state’s governor since 2019, and Kansas voters in 2022 voted decisively to defeat a proposed state constitutional amendment that would have declared that residents did not have any right to an abortion.

GOP strategists began raising alarms about Republican Sen. Roger Marshall’s reelection prospects months ago, warning that he wasn’t popular among independents or Democrats and that even Republican voters have mixed opinions about him.

Marshall, one of the president’s most loyal allies, has had to battle negative publicity after The New York Times reported that the incumbent senator, who is a doctor and co-owner of an OB-GYN medical practice, sued 700 patients for medical debts.

He is running against Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton, a popular megachurch pastor who has a knack for getting his message across and has pledged he will not support Schumer for Democratic leader but instead work with fellow centrists to get things done in Washington.

The Cook Political Report rates the Kansas Senate race a “toss-up,” and Hamilton has a narrow 2-point lead in recent polls, according to the DDHQ average.

South Carolina was expected to be a slam dunk for Republicans until the sudden death of longtime Sen. Lindsey Graham (R), which set up a contentious battle for the Republican nomination between his sister, Darline Graham, who had Trump’s backing, and conservative Rep. Ralph Norman.

Like in Texas, bruised Republican feelings haven’t healed in the aftermath of the race as Norman recently panned Graham, telling CNN that she was “propped up by special interest groups.”

Graham has a famous last name but not much experience in policy and politics.

She stumbled at a Republican debate in August when she admitted that “I’m not that informed on national security” — a shocking admission from a candidate whose late brother was a preeminent voice on defense matters in Congress.

Graham was tagged by opponents in the Senate GOP primary as a mystery candidate who couldn’t be counted on to deliver on a conservative agenda if elected to a full term. But she has had Trump’s strong support, and that means a lot in a state the president won by nearly 18 percentage points in 2024.

Democrats think that their nominee, pediatrician Annie Andrews, presents a good contrast with Graham because she can talk about how the expiration of expanded health insurance premium subsidies under the Affordable Care Act and cuts to Medicaid will impact children and families.

A recent New York Times/Siena poll of 707 South Carolina voters showed the race deadlocked, with Graham and Andrews each having 48-percent support.

The Cook Political Report rates the race as “lean Republican.”

Minnesota has been a reliably Democratic state over the years. The last Republican from there to win election to the U.S. Senate was Sen. Norm Coleman in 2002.

Republicans think they have a great candidate in former journalist and sportscaster Michele Tafoya.

Democrats had to coalesce after the hard-fought primary contest between Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, the progressive, and Rep. Angie Craig (D-Minn.), the centrist.

Democratic sources said the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee initially viewed Craig as the stronger candidate in a general election.

Republicans may have a better chance of swiping the Minnesota Senate seat, held by retiring Democratic Sen. Tina Smith, because of lingering fallout over the $250 million to $350 million public benefits fraud scandal that happened on Democratic Gov. Tim Walz’s watch.

Even so, it would be a major upset for Republicans to win the Senate race in Minnesota when Trump’s job approval rating in the state is 37 percent and his disapproval rating is 62 percent, according to a recent KSTP/Survey USA poll.

The Cook Political Report rates Minnesota as “lean Democrat.”

articles.title: Democrats are on the brink of a blue tsunami, if the polls are right
articles.summary: A series of new polls suggest things are breaking for Democrats in the battles for the House and Senate, even as experts warn that the polling can be off and a sweep is not set in stone. New York Times/Siena polls released Sunday night showed Democrats ahead in seven Senate battlegrounds, including an 11-point advantage…
articles.body:
A series of new polls suggest things are breaking for Democrats in the battles for the House and Senate, even as experts warn that the polling can be off and a sweep is not set in stone.

New York Times/Siena polls released Sunday night showed Democrats ahead in seven Senate battlegrounds, including an 11-point advantage in Michigan and a 7-point lead in Texas.

Democrats were also up in Maine, Ohio, Kansas, Alaska and Iowa, though their candidates’ leads in those races were within the margin of error.

The party needs to net just four Senate seats to win the majority, meaning that if those numbers bear out, Democrats are barreling toward what could be the blue tsunami of their dreams. The Senate results also foretell a big win in the House that might help the party win a large majority in that chamber.

As of Monday, forecasts from Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) gave Democrats an 84 percent chance of winning the House, and a slimmer — but climbing — 65 percent probability of taking the Senate majority.

Political analyst Nate Silver predicted a “blue tsunami” in light of the new numbers.

He argued in his newsletter that the results “resolve” some ambiguity about the prediction that “polls show that the Democrats will win the Senate, perhaps soundly.”

The polls “might be wrong or they might predict slightly the wrong states to flip,” Silver wrote. “But Democrats could actually absorb a modest-sized polling error and perhaps still prevail given the latest round of surveys.”

All that said, Democrats have been disappointed by polls before, and the party has also seen some bad headlines in the last week, including the decision by Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) on Sunday to endorse GOP candidate Mike Rogers in Michigan’s Senate race over the Democrat who defeated her in the primary, Abdul El-Sayed.

That gave Republicans some new hope of winning a Senate seat away from Democrats. The GOP also sees its chances of winning Alaska growing amid the controversy surrounding reports that Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola’s campaign was involved in recruiting Daniel J. Sullivan to run for Senate against the incumbent Republican senator, who is also named Dan Sullivan.

Polls in the Trump era have notably overestimated Democratic support in the last three presidential elections, according to Silver’s analysis , including a 4.7-point miss across major contests in 2020. And there’s an enduring concern that Democrats are more likely to take part in surveys.

The New York Times Times also offered a caveat for their latest findings, noting the possibility “that nonresponse bias is worse than ever” and that “if so, polls could seriously underestimate Republicans once again.”

Still, the Times’s Nate Cohn, like Silver, contended that “Democrats lead by enough that they could win the Senate even if the polls underestimate Republicans by as much as they did in 2016 or 2020.”

The Times also noted that they updated their methodology earlier this year and found that their 2024 polls would have been more accurate on average with it in place. If the latest batch of polls had been tabulated with the old weighting systems, Democrats would have performed even better .

Democrats’ 11-point advantage in Michigan, for example, would climb to a 16-point edge. In Alaska, the current 1-point margin would be 6 points. In Texas, a 7-point edge would climb to 9 points.

“This would seem to be another indication of what we’re seeing broadly, which is that Democrats are at least somewhat favored to flip the Senate,” Geoffrey Skelley, DDHQ’s chief elections analyst, said of the polls.

“A Republican Senate is still quite possible, much more possible than a Republican House at this point. But you know, this is more polling good news for Democrats.”

DDHQ’s polling averages show El-Sayed with a 5-point lead over Rogers. In Texas, the averages have Democrat James Talarico up 3.5 points over Republican Ken Paxton.

The new Times/Siena polling paints an even brighter picture for the party in both vital states, showing El-Sayed with 53 percent to Rogers’s 42 percent in Michigan — and Talarico with 50 percent to Paxton’s 43 percent in Texas.

In Maine, Sen. Susan Collins (R) was trailing Democratic challenger Troy Jackson by 6 points, with 45 percent to 51 percent, respectively.

Sen. Jon Husted (R) was behind former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D) by 5 points in Ohio, with 44 percent to 49 percent. It was the same split in Kansas, where Sen. Roger Marshall (R) faces Democrat Adam Hamilton.

In Alaska, Peltola was 2 points ahead of incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan, with 48 to the Republican’s 46 percent.

The closest state in the new polling was Iowa, where Democrat Josh Turek had a 1-point edge on Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson.

Skelley said the new numbers, though eye-popping, haven’t “dramatically moved” DDHQ’s polling averages.

“The Michigan result is probably the one true outlier of this bunch, compared to previous polling in these races … but the other ones were not really necessarily different from some other polling we’ve had in this race,” he added, pointing to other recent polls out of Texas that have shown Talarico up by a similar margin.

In the run-up to a high-stakes election, some have suggested that the polls signal either a major blue wave — or a blow to the polling industry, which voters already distrust as President Trump claims the unfavorable numbers are “ fake .”

“The truth is probably somewhere in between,” Skelley said. “Obviously, if they are generally understating Republican support and Republicans eke out wins in a bunch of these key races, we’ll be able to say, well, there was a systematic error that understated Republican performance. More likely, it’s going to vary a lot from state to state.”

Skelley pointed out that the half-dozen most competitive Senate contests this cycle are in red states and stressed that election observers should look at the landscape of each state as well as the polling margins.

In Texas, for example, “knowing that the average undecided voter in Texas is Republican-leaning, I think we can expect Paxton to be finishing higher,” he said.

“But it is good news for Talarico that in a number of polls he’s now hitting 49-50 percent because that’s where he needs to be to have a chance of winning, and you don’t tend to see candidates vastly underperform where their average support is.”

Libertarian candidates are also on the ballot in some key races, including in Texas and Kansas, and could throw a wrench into the works even if they draw single-digit support.

All told, Democrats need to net four seats to flip the Senate.

The three Senate races that DDHQ considers toss-ups — Iowa, Kansas and Ohio — are all Republican-held seats, and Democrats are narrowly favored in the latter two.

Three more races that were considered toss-ups last week — Alaska, Maine and Texas — have all since shifted to “lean” Democratic.

“I really do think it speaks to the GOP’s issues now that they just basically have to hope for a polling error,” Skelley said.

Democrats are leading by almost 10 points on a generic congressional ballot, according to DDHQ’s latest polling averages, and Trump’s approval rating has spent the last several weeks around 20 points underwater.

“Historically, it would not be weird for the party with a president that unpopular to lose badly in a midterm, even seats that were otherwise expected to be favorable.”

articles.title: The House races to watch for early signs of a midterm wave
articles.summary: The House battlefield in Tuesday’s midterms comprises dozens of races in largely purple districts where majorities are won and lost. But as GOP leaders scramble against the odds to salvage their fragile majority — and the favored Democrats fight to run up the score — both sides are paying particular attention to a much smaller…
articles.body:
The House battlefield in Tuesday’s midterms comprises dozens of races in largely purple districts where majorities are won and lost.

But as GOP leaders scramble against the odds to salvage their fragile majority — and the favored Democrats fight to run up the score — both sides are paying particular attention to a much smaller number of contests that might lend early hints about where the winds are blowing and whether a wave is forming.

Many of those races are on the East Coast, where the polls close first and the results are expected to arrive most quickly. But other districts have unique demographic characteristics that can reveal broader trends about which voters are animated, which are staying home, and how those dynamics might affect the overall results.

Here are the races that outside experts and campaign operatives in both parties will be watching most closely as a gauge of where the momentum is flowing on election night.

There are three races in Virginia that are competitive, to varying degrees, and experts are monitoring all three of them closely for telltale signs of broader trends.

In the 2nd District around Virginia Beach, GOP Rep. Jen Kiggans is facing a tough challenge from former Rep. Elaine Luria (D), who held the seat for two terms before Kiggans picked her off in 2022. Both candidates are Navy veterans, and both are well known among voters. Republicans see the race as an early gauge of how their battleground incumbents will fare.

“That is the bellwether district in my view,” said a Republican campaign operative. “You have a well-funded incumbent going against a former member, who also has high name ID and [is] very well funded. So that will be a true test, early in the night, on how our incumbents are holding up.”

Virginia’s 1st District is also under a microscope. The seat is held by GOP Rep. Rob Wittman, a 20-year House veteran who was initially expected to skate to victory in a district President Trump won by 5 points in 2024. But the contest has tightened considerably in the final stretch, and the analysts at Sabato’s Crystal Ball, an independent election handicapper based at the University of Virginia, say the race now leans in favor of the Democratic challenger Shannon Taylor, the top prosecutor for Henrico County.

In an even greater sign of the GOP’s struggles this cycle, Republican Rep. John McGuire, a close ally of the president, is also facing stiff headwinds in the 5th District, which Trump won by 12 points just two years ago. The analysts at the Cook Political Report rate the race a toss-up. And on Monday, Sabato shifted the race in favor of the Democratic challenger, former Rep. Tom Perriello, who held the seat from 2009 to 2011.

If Perriello wins, “then the floor has fallen out from underneath Republicans,” said a Democratic campaign strategist.

Kyle Kondik, the managing editor of Sabato’s Crystal Ball, agreed. He said if Democrats defeat Kiggans, it would suggest they’ll win control of the House; if they beat Wittman, it would signal an even greater shift in power around the country; and if McGuire falls, it would suggest a “Dem megawave.”

The district comprising Lansing has been a bellwether battleground for years. The seat was held by Sen. Elissa Slotkin, a centrist Democrat, before she jumped to the Senate last year and was replaced by moderate Republican Rep. Tom Barrett, an Army veteran.

Now Democrats are hoping the current political environment will help them make Barrett a one-term lawmaker. Challenging him is William Lawrence, a liberal climate activist who, until recently , was a member of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA).

That affiliation has sparked plenty of attacks from Republicans, who say Lawrence is simply too liberal for the purple 7th District. But they also say the outcome will be a good gauge of where voters are nationally — and whether Trump is a greater liability, for Republicans, than the socialist label is for Democrats.

“William Lawrence is literally a member of the DSA. And so that’s another test of: Do these further-to-the-left candidates — does that candidate-quality thing even matter?” said the GOP campaign strategist. “That’s a really good seat to look at to get a sense of how the night goes.”

Democrats like their chances, noting that Lawrence was one of the first candidates this cycle to tap into the widespread outrage over data centers, which has transcended region and party. He’s proposing a national 12-month moratorium on building them.

“He has made data centers a central part of his pitch. I think he’s also somebody who is definitely in tune with the anger that folks have on the ground in Michigan,” said the Democratic strategist. “Michigan 7 is just always close, always a toss-up no matter what. And we feel good about our chances there right now.”

Texas was the first GOP-led state to redraw its House map this cycle, and Republicans did it with designs to pick up five Democratic seats, largely in the south near the Mexican border. Trump made inroads with Hispanic voters in 2024, and the new lines sought to exploit that shift.

But polls indicate that Hispanic voters have soured on Trump , largely over his deportation surge, and Texas will test just how angry those voters are — and how far a potential backlash might reach.

The shift has already helped several Democratic incumbents, including Reps. Henry Cuellar in the 28th District and Vicente Gonzalez in the 34th, who appear poised to survive a redistricting process that had targeted them directly.

“I’ll be honest, [in] South Texas, the bottom has fallen out,” the GOP operative said. “Vicente Gonzalez looked like one of the most appetizing pickups for us, and I still do think we can get that race close. But I think with the ICE raids and the economy, especially in South Texas, it really hit us hardest.”

The shift has been so pronounced that Democrats are now fighting to pick off at least one Republican incumbent, Rep. Monica De La Cruz, in the 15th District, and they’re increasingly optimistic they can keep the 35th District, which was redrawn to eliminate Democratic Rep. Greg Casar. Cook rates both races as toss-ups, while Sabato puts both in the “leans Democrat” column.

“Those are the ones to keep an eye on for how much of a backlash is there to the Trump administration’s overstep when it comes to ICE enforcement,” said the Democratic operative, using an abbreviation for Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

In redrawing their House map this year at Trump’s behest, Republicans in North Carolina’s state House had a particular target in mind: Rep. Don Davis, a two-term Democrat who represents the northeastern corner of the state.

But the new map wasn’t the knockout blow Republicans had envisioned, and in recent weeks Davis’s prospects have improved for the Democrats, who are also hoping to pick up a Senate seat in the Tar Heel State. Cook rates the race a toss-up, while Sabato gives Davis a slight edge.

“He’s very moderate, he’s very well known around the district, and we always knew that was going to be really tough,” the GOP operative acknowledged.

The contest is being viewed as an early bellwether of the Republicans’ broader redistricting campaign. But in a district with a large Black population, it’s also being watched closely for signs of how Black voters — who shifted toward Trump in 2024 — have responded to the president’s subsequent efforts to eliminate Black districts and gut the Voting Rights Act, a seminal law of the Civil Rights Movement.

A Davis victory, the Democratic strategist said, would indicate “there’s significant backlash among Black voters in the South, which could help us in other places.” That includes Alabama’s 2nd District, where Republicans sought to draw Rep. Shomari Figures (D) out of office.

The Keystone State is home to four battleground districts where GOP incumbents are fighting to keep their seats. How those races turn out, the experts say, will reveal much about the mood of American voters more broadly.

“If we lose all four of them, that’s the majority right there. And that’ll tell you how the margins are going to look,” said the Republican strategist. “Pennsylvania will be the gauge of how bad it’s going to be in terms of how many districts we actually lose altogether.”

Three of those contests are particularly challenging for Republicans this cycle. Reps. Ryan Mackenzie in the 7th District, Rob Bresnahan in the 8th and Scott Perry in the 10th are all predicted to lose to their Democratic opponents, according to the analysts at Cook and Sabato.

In the 1st District, Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick is faring slightly better: Cook rates his race a toss-up. But Sabato analysts gave Democrats the edge in the race in the final hours before voters go to the polls.

Democrats acknowledge that Fitzpatrick, a centrist who has done more than most Republicans to distance himself from Trump, will be tough to beat. But even Republicans aren’t guaranteeing victory.

For several cycles straight, Democrats have tried unsuccessfully to pick off several Republican incumbents in Iowa. How they fare this year might lend hints about the size of a blue wave, or if one arrives at all.

Republicans say they’re confident that GOP Rep. Zach Nunn will win his right to a third term in the 3rd District, despite analysts predicting that Democrats will steal that seat on Tuesday. And they like their chances of keeping the 2nd District, which was vacated by GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson, who’s running for Senate.

But the outcome of those races will hinge on turnout for Hinson in the Senate race, which could make or break the vulnerable House GOP candidates on the ballot below her.

“If she does well on the Senate side of things, I do think Nunn’s in good shape — and her open seat, as well in Iowa 2,” said the Republican campaign strategist.

Republicans are less confident about another Iowa Republican, Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks in the 1st District, who is among the most vulnerable incumbent Republicans of the cycle.

“I wouldn’t read too much into Miller-Meeks losing, because I think it’s just bound to happen,” said the GOP operative. “I think the better gauge is Nunn, where if he holds on, it’s going to be a pretty decent night for us.”

Another early-results state is Florida, where the GOP-led Legislature redrew its House map with designs to flip four Democratic seats. Kondik, the managing editor of Sabato’s Crystal Ball, said the outcome of those races will predict who controls the House next year.

“See how many gerrymandered seats in Florida Dems salvage,” he said. “Saving at least one is consistent with winning the House.”

The redistricting effort is expected to yield at least some results for the GOP: Democratic Rep. Darren Soto is predicted to lose his seat in the 9th District after a decade on Capitol Hill. And Republicans are optimistic they will pick up the seats held by the other Democrats targeted by the new map, including Reps. Kathy Castor in the 14th District, Jared Moskowitz in the 25th and an open seat left vacant by the retiring Rep. Lois Frankel in the 22nd.

“Hispanic voters care less about the ICE raids and more about the socialism message,” said the Republican strategist. “I feel really good about the Florida seats. … I think we’ll come out on top in almost all of them.”

But as in the other redistricted states, polls suggest the effort is falling short of initial expectations. Moskowitz, for instance, is now favored in his race, according to both Cook and Sabato. And both handicappers rate Castor’s seat and Frankel’s open seat up for grabs.

articles.title: Supreme Court weighs if Colorado preschools must admit kids of same-sex couples
articles.summary: The Supreme Court will hear oral arguments Tuesday on whether Colorado can require preschools that accept public dollars to admit the children of same-sex couples. It’s the latest battle at the intersection of religious and LGBTQ rights to reach the justices. The Archdiocese of Denver, a group of Catholic parishes and parents Daniel and Lisa…
articles.body:
The Supreme Court will hear oral arguments Tuesday on whether Colorado can require preschools that accept public dollars to admit the children of same-sex couples.

It’s the latest battle at the intersection of religious and LGBTQ rights to reach the justices.

The Archdiocese of Denver, a group of Catholic parishes and parents Daniel and Lisa Sheley challenge Colorado’s antidiscrimination mandate under the First Amendment.

“The inevitable result of Colorado’s thumb on the scale is that more Colorado children will be funneled toward preschools that share Colorado’s perspective on matters of sex and marriage,” they wrote in court filings.

Coincidentally, the high-stakes arguments land as millions of Americans head to the polls on Election Day, with voters in several states set to consider LGBTQ-related ballot measures.

A decision in the Colorado case is expected by summer.

First implemented in 2023, Colorado funds 15 hours of universal pre-K per week for each eligible child. Parents can choose where to send their child, and more than 2,000 preschools applied to participate in the program this year.

Participating schools must agree to provide families an “equal opportunity” to enroll regardless of various criteria, including sexual orientation and gender identity.

That’s a problem for St. Mary Catholic Parish, the preschool leading the charge at the Supreme Court.

Before enrolling a child at the school, parents must sign a statement of “Community Beliefs and Commitments.” It requires families to “display a positive and supportive attitude toward the Catholic Church” and its teachings, including its stances against abortion and same-sex marriage. Families “must refrain from public promotion or approval of any conduct” that would discredit those teachings.

Colorado contends its mandate is constitutional and the school should be forced to comply if it wants to receive public funds.

“Whatever a family’s publicly funded preschool options—however many or few—Colorado seeks to ensure those options are not limited by that family’s protected-class status,” the state wrote in court filings.

Colorado’s LGBTQ protections don’t have a great track record before the conservative-majority Supreme Court. In recent terms, the justices ruled for a counselor who challenged the state’s “conversion therapy” ban and a website designer and cake baker who separately challenged Colorado’s mandate that they perform their work for same-sex weddings, too.

The newest case is legally distinct from those battles, however. The preschool dispute provides the court a chance to narrow a key 1990 Supreme Court precedent that several of the court’s conservatives have criticized for being incompatible with religious liberty.

The archdiocese hopes the court will do so. Preschool enrollment has already declined almost 20 percent across the archdiocese since Colorado began its universal pre-K program, court filings indicate.

Represented by the Becket Fund for Religious Liberty, the archdiocese points to how the state allows preschools that specifically serve low-income families and students with disabilities to participate.

“Petitioners have no objection to Colorado’s decision to allow over 1,000 UPK preschools to selectively serve the communities they are designed to serve—Petitioners simply want the same accommodation extended to them,” the group wrote in court filings, using an acronym for universal pre-K.

It’s an argument backed by roughly 20 Republican-led states, nearly four dozen Republican members of Congress, the Union of Orthodox Jewish Congregations of America and a handful of other religious groups. The Trump administration also agrees and will argue the case alongside the schools on Tuesday.

Colorado’s defense, meanwhile, is supported by the NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund, nearly 180 Democrats in Congress, LGBTQ advocacy groups and the Freedom From Religious Foundation.

“Petitioners’ theory, at its core, threatens to replace the considered judgment of legislatures with ad hoc exemptions. That would permit litigants to become laws unto themselves,” the lawmakers wrote to the justices.
