articles.title: Democrats ready for blame game, whatever actually happens today
articles.summary: The giddy mix of anticipation and despair that Democrats are experiencing today should be familiar to them. It’s the old “nauseously optimistic” feeling that has been their lot in every election since 2016. All the dashboard indicators point toward big gains for the blue team in Congress and state capitols from coast to coast, but,…
articles.body:
The giddy mix of anticipation and despair that Democrats are experiencing today should be familiar to them. It’s the old “nauseously optimistic” feeling that has been their lot in every election since 2016.

All the dashboard indicators point toward big gains for the blue team in Congress and state capitols from coast to coast, but, of course, that’s what they thought when Hillary Clinton was atop the ticket a decade ago. Even as they contemplate races that would have sounded laughable just a few months ago — battlegrounds in Mississippi and South Carolina or blue Kansas — Democrats can’t escape the dreadful fear that it’s all a mirage.

Indeed, those raised expectations may lead to a sense of disappointment, even if Democrats have what should be seen as a successful midterm. As one big-time party operative, a veteran of two presidential campaigns now knee-deep in Senate races this cycle, put it to me, “Another Ted Lasso election. It’s the hope that kills you.”

But for most Democrats, the line between success and failure is pretty straightforward: Either Democrats will win back the Senate or they won’t. A Democratic House being a foregone conclusion in the minds of members of both parties, a Senate majority stands as the pass-fail test for a party still stinging from its 2024 defeat.

Democratic nominee Roy Cooper, the former governor of North Carolina, is expected to prevail in his state, inching Democrats closer to their goal.

Can Democrats win four of the seven remaining Senate toss-up seats in Maine, Ohio, Michigan, Iowa, Kansas, Texas and Alaska? Even supposing a midterm polling miss on par with the largest of the century — the 2006 surveys that, taken together, understated Republican support by about 3 points nationally — Democrats lead in an adjusted average of high-quality polls in every one of those battlegrounds except for Iowa. Without weighting for a big polling miss, Democrats lead in all seven.

If the blue team ends up with 53 of 54 Senate seats, it won’t matter to rank-and-file Democrats whether the beautiful dream of flipping South Carolina or Mississippi never comes to pass. They would be too busy celebrating the first Democratic senator elected by Texas since 1988 — who’d also be the first nonincumbent since 1970.

And just like in 2006 when the polls may have missed but Democrats still flipped both chambers with lots of red-state victories, the party’s current base would feel similarly emboldened about the next presidential cycle. Would Democrats have been so willing to throw over Clinton — nearly a prohibitive favorite when the 2008 cycle began — for then-Sen. Barack Obama had their party not just flipped Senate seats in Montana, Missouri, Ohio, Virginia (then still a red state) and Pennsylvania? Probably not. A great midterm for Democrats would make primary voters less risk-averse and more willing to take a chance on an inspirational but untested choice.

The line for the next “generational political talent” would stretch around the block.

So, what if this year’s blue wave crashes into a red wall? To hold the Senate, Republicans would need to see an average polling miss bigger than any of the presidential years when President Trump was on the ballot. But, hey, we don’t have a ton of great state-level polling, especially in seldom-surveyed places like Alaska and Kansas. Plus, Elon Musk has spent something on the order of a half-billion dollars to keep the Senate for his party. If the Republicans narrowly manage to keep a majority, maybe even with the help of a party-switching Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.), what would the 2028 Democratic electorate think?

First would come the bitter recriminations. Imagine a world where Michigan made the difference and Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) became the villain of a narrative about how moderates — especially pro-Israel moderates — are to blame for the unmet expectations of 2026. Or, the counterargument from the mainstream that democratic socialists and the far left foisted candidates like Abdul El-Sayed and Troy Jackson on unwilling general electorates and cost the party its chance to make the most of 2026. If today feels like a bust to Democrats, it’s going to make the opening act of the coming presidential contest that much uglier.

Whom that would help in the longer run, we can’t know for sure. The already radicalizing left wing would grow in intensity and, therefore, power. “We tried it your way,” they would say, “now we’re going full Robespierre.” But, a miss this week would also chasten early-state primary voters and lead them to believe that safer candidates — the kind that succeeded in places like North Carolina and Georgia — are the way to go. Perhaps that’s a world in which a California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) or another establishment pick would seem prudent. Would Democrats even become willing to think about a red-state moderate if they thought it would finally bring back the long-lost “blue wall” states?

Remember the lessons of recent primary elections in the Democratic Party: The political professionals and the activist core are substantially to the left of the party’s median voter. Certainly, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) or another progressive populist with a committed, compact plurality could roll through a crowded field in the same way Trump did in 2016.

But, Democrats in the 2010s and 2020s have typically been better at strategic voting than Republicans. For all the talk of the rise in socialism and radicalism, a look across the party’s battleground-state offerings mostly shows a party willing to try to give persuadable voters what they appear to want.

Does that fade with Trump as a lame duck? Democrats, rightly or wrongly, don’t think that Vice President Vance will make a formidable opponent in 2028. Perhaps without the threat of Trump, Democratic leaders will find primary voters unwilling to think about electability. After all, given the track record of “safe” choices in 2016 and 2024, voters may just be ready to let their freak flags fly, whatever happens today.

But make no mistake, that process begins today, and it starts with a struggle over claiming credit or placing blame over the results that Democrats right now are so nauseously optimistic about.

articles.title: A tale of two political ads
articles.summary: What we will remember from this season are the two ads the ended it — and possibly ended the political aspirations of some would-be politicians.
articles.body:
It’s finally election day after a long and bruising campaign season. Regardless of who ends up controlling the House and the Senate, this election season will be remembered for two ads, one from the Right and one from the Left, which defined it by finding new lows in American politics. Yet they also revealed that many Americans—on either side—had found their floor in terms of what they would tolerate from people seeking office.

The first ad was put out by the Republican candidate for governor in Ohio, Vivek Ramaswamy. The ad featured the biological mother of his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton, calling her daughter a liar. It seemed like powerful stuff, until you learned the backstory: Acton’s mother has not seen her daughter since Amy was 12. That’s when Amy accused her stepfather of raping her.

Rather than stand by her own daughter, Acton’s mother stood by her alleged rapist, fleeing the state with him after an indictment was handed down and a warrant issued for his arrest, and staying with him until his death.

That is the woman Ramaswamy trotted out as an authority on Acton’s truth telling: a woman who stayed with her daughter’s alleged rapist, abandoning her child at the tender age of 12 to do so.

The ad initially appeared on social media. At first, it wasn’t clear who had released it, leading many Republicans to condemn the ad and to urge Ramaswamy to do the same. Yet it turned out that Ramaswamy’s campaign was actually responsible for the ad — indeed, Ramaswamy himself pushed for the ad over the objections of his staff.

To cut the ad, an agency called The Strategy Group tracked Acton’s mother down to a church parking lot, where she was living in her car with a bunch of cats. Some of Ramaswamy’s staffers felt uncomfortable with the state of Acton’s mother, who did not appear well. Ramaswamy overruled them, slapping his name on the ad and airing it on television throughout Ohio. When criticized for it, he doubled and tripled down on the ad, insisting that Acton’s mother was fair game, and he was joined in this efforts by Vice President JD Vance and President Trump himself.

It was utterly depraved to make the ad, air it, and defend it. The ad weaponized the child rape of his opponent for naked political gain. It was the kind of thing many Americans assumed was utterly beneath even the most contemptible politician in America.

But if we were wrong to expect politicians like Ramaswamy to have anything close to a moral compass, we were not wrong about our fellow Americans. Ramaswamy had already been trailing Acton in the polls when the ad came out, but his polling cratered afterward. The ad was nothing short of an October surprise planted by Ramaswamy against himself — the nail in the coffin of any political aspirations he might have going forward. And not a minute too soon.

The American people had found their floor of what they would no longer tolerate.

Something similar happened on the Left with an ad that came out in support of the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed. The wasn’t put out by El Sayed’s campaign but by YouTuber Cenk Uygur’s left-wing political action committee, Rebellion PAC. The ad featured a couple in a grocery store choosing items for their children, and having to put them back one after another because the money for bananas had to go instead to “killing Palestinians.” It ended by riffing off another famous ad from 2024: “Mike Rogers is for they/them” — with pictures of Israeli politicians — ”Abdul El-Sayed is for you.”

The ad was widely denounced as antisemitic, including by many Democrats, who pointed out how the ad sought to blame Jews for the fact that you can’t afford to feed your kids. Many called on El-Sayed to condemn the ad, but when he addressed it, he did so in a mealy-mouthed way that left many wanting: His campaign put out a statement saying the ad was “not affiliated in any way” with him or his candidacy. and “no one speaks for Abdul but himself and his campaign.”

That is not, as many pointed out, a condemnation of the ad. It is in fact the opposite—a refusal to denounce a message that scapegoats Jews for Michigan’s problems.

El-Sayed didn’t wat the negative consequences, but he couldn’t honestly condemn the ad; after all, as his primary challenger, Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), pointed out, El Sayed had repeatedly made the same argument dramatized in the ad throughout his campaign. He blamed taxpayer aid to Israel for everything from Michigan’s failing schools to its failing health care. It was of a piece with his choice to campaign five times with Uyghur’s nephew, the Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, who compared Jews to the Ku Klux Klan last week and said American deserved 9/11. Piker, too, was someone El-Sayed repeatedly refused to denounce.

El-Sayed later said he “disagreed” with the contents of the ad, but he was not pressed to explain how. Inquiring minds want to know.

Stevens had been invited to appear alongside El-Sayed at a campaign event on Sunday. She stipulated as a condition of her appearance that he denounce both the ad and his own rhetoric, which had engaged in similar scapegoating of Jews. In response, El-Sayed told Stevens to take a hike, which she did — right over to his Republican opponent Mike Rogers’ campaign.

Like many Republicans in Ohio sick to their stomachs over Ramaswamy’s ad, Haley Stevens had found her floor.

We will find out soon the results of the midterms. But what we will remember from this season are the two ads the ended it — and possibly ended the political aspirations of some would-be politicians.

Batya Ungar Sargon is the host of “ Batya !” which airs Saturday nights at 7 p.m. Eastern Time on NewsNation, the nation’s fastest-growing cable news network and a sister company of The Hill.

articles.title: The Hill’s election night cheat sheet
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ What to know as polls close ▪ Trump gives final pitch ▪ What’s next for Haley Stevens? ▪ Will Iran strikes resume? After a long, tense and sometimes drama-filled campaign cycle, Election Day is finally here. What are the pivotal races? When will we know the outcomes? How much sleep do…
articles.body:
After a long, tense and sometimes drama-filled campaign cycle, Election Day is finally here.

What are the pivotal races? When will we know the outcomes? How much sleep do you need to function on Wednesday? We’ll answer these questions and more in our election night cheat sheet, with some help from our friends at Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) .

What’s on the line tonight? Just the course of President Trump ‘s final two years in office and the future of both parties.

Once polls close, starting at 6 p.m. EST, results will start coming in rapid-fire moving west. If there’s a “blue tsunami,” as some are predicting, we could know the result within hours. If it’s closer than polls predict, it could take days.

Here’s what to keep an eye on as polls close and returns come in.

Democrats are overwhelming favorites to win control of the House. The forecast from DDHQ has ticked up even more in the cycle’s final days, reaching 84 percent ahead of Election Day.

Some of the earliest polls to close will give a hint of whether a Democratic wave will turn into a tsunami or a ripple.

One of the first places to watch, right as the first polls close at 6 p.m., is Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District. Rep. Andy Barr (R-Ky.) is vacating the seat to run for governor, and Democrats have expressed some hope that the district could be in play.

Democrats don’t need to win the seat to signal a good night for them. But if Democrat Zach Dembo can stay competitive, that could be a good sign for his party.

In Indiana’s 5th Congressional District, Rep. Victoria Spartz (R) is expected to hang on, but a strong Democratic performance in the Indianapolis suburbs could be telling.

When 7 p.m. rolls around, all eyes will be on Florida’s 14th and 25th districts, which are prime pickup targets for Republicans after the state’s mid-decade redistricting left Democratic Reps. Kathy Castor and Jared Moskowitz with tougher fights. Flipping either seat would be a sign that Republicans are holding their own.

In Virginia, Rep. Jen Kiggans (R) is a key target for Democrats, and her fate could signal the direction of the rest of the night.

Democrats are favored to win Senate majority, but barely. Each state’s vote-counting procedures will play a key role in how the night develops.

Democrats’ most-likely pickup seems to be North Carolina, a state that is known to count votes fast. Results from Georgia and Florida will also likely come earlier in the night. A Democratic win in Florida would be bad news for Republicans nationwide.

If Democrats flip North Carolina and oust Sen. Susan Collins (R) in Maine — a state former Vice President Kamala Harris won in 2024 — attention will likely quickly shift to Ohio and Texas. But Texas’s slow-counting Harris County could delay a race call if the contest is razor-tight.

Based on DDHQ’s forecast, Ohio may end up being the clincher. All other things equal, the odds of Senate control swing hard toward whichever party wins the Buckeye State — and it may signal the political winds in Iowa and Kansas too.

Democrats are favored to win 51 seats, including Alaska, where the last polls won’t close until 1 a.m. EST. If Ohio or another tossup state flips before then, Senate control could be decided before the Last Frontier declares a winner.

It depends on two key factors: when you go to sleep and how close key races are. If Democrats pull off big wins, control of both chambers could be called before midnight eastern.

The House is considerably more likely to be clear sooner than the Senate, as Democrats only need to net a few seats to win a majority in the lower chamber.

If the main battlegrounds are close, this could drag into Wednesday. Texas and Michigan could still be counting ballots well into the night, and if no candidate wins a majority in the first round of ranked choice voting in Maine and Alaska, it could be weeks before we have a winner.

Vote counting in Maine could take up to two weeks, according to the state government . And Alaska accepts ballots for up to 15 days after Election Day, meaning the counting could stretch into mid-November. And with the legal and political scrutiny surrounding the race, a final decision could take even longer.

This drawn-out scenario is unlikely, but not impossible.

Of note, the Senate was called for the GOP by The Associated Press at 12:06 a.m. in 2024. But it wasn’t called until four days later in 2022.

The House was called for Democrats at 3 a.m. in 2018, but the call in each cycle since then took at least a week.

Expect a night of excitement and surprises either way. The Hill’s Julia Mueller dives into five Senate races that could provide upset victories to an underdog. Insiders can read more here .

▪ The Hill : Your hour-by-hour guide to the midterms.

▪ The Hill : House races to watch for early signs of a midterm wave.

▪ The Hill Insider : Why Democrats can survive a polling miss.

Thousands of voters in Washoe County, Nev., received mail-in ballot return envelopes with a printing error that included the word “FALSE” on them. A spokesperson said about 32,000 envelopes were affected, and the error wasn’t limited to any political party. They said the issue was identified and corrected in subsequent batches of envelopes.

Snap Inc., the parent company of Snapchat, has settled claims alleging the platform was intentionally designed to be addictive for young users, joining fellow tech giant Meta in settling the case from a woman who alleged she was harmed by their products. The deal’s details remain confidential and came two days before a scheduled trial.

The U.S. plans to mediate another round of talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi next week , special envoy Steve Witkoff said. He added that U.S. negotiators would meet with NATO allies this week to discuss security guarantees for Ukraine and supporting the country’s reconstruction.

President Trump speaks in front of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and Washington Monument, Nov. 2, 2026, in Washington. (Mark Schiefelbein, Associated Press)

FINAL REFLECTION: The president used his final speech to the public before Election Day to announce the reopening of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and to tout other changes around the nation’s capital, only mentioning the midterm elections roughly 20 minutes into his remarks.

“As you know, this is the last day before the midterm elections, the most important midterm I believe in our lifetime,” he said. “The Democrat Party has nominated the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history. These are the most dangerous candidates ever put up.”

The president pointed to several candidates, including Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed , repeating claims about potential ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, and the rogue candidate Dan Sullivan in Alaska running against the incumbent senator with the same name.

Trump touted his achievements over the last two years, saying, “I’ve kept every single promise I made, except far more,” and he repeated his promise that he would give American adults a $5,000 check if Republicans win the midterms.

But he also seemed to acknowledge the unfavorable odds Republicans face.

“For some reason, the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot,” he said.

▪ The Hill : Forecasts of midterm blue wave put Trump’s legacy on line.

▪ The Hill Insider : 10 Senate seats most likely to flip.

DISPUTED VOTES: The Supreme Court swiftly rejected the Trump administration’s effort to force California officials to set aside roughly 20,000 ballots that the federal government claims belong to people suspected of being noncitizens.

The court’s one-sentence order did not include an explanation and had no noted dissents. It came hours after the Trump administration filed an emergency appeal with the high court after California persuaded lower courts that the administration has no authority to force the state to verify those voters’ citizenship.

The administration had warned that the clock was running out. All sides agreed that ballots could not be separated once they were processed, and election officials already received hundreds of thousands of mail ballots ahead of Election Day.

▪ The Hill : Data analysts flag mismatches in administration’s eligible list.

▪ The Hill : Judge blocks DOJ from threatening election officials.

BATTLE OF RIGHTS: The Supreme Court will hear arguments today in a major case that pits religious liberty against LGBTQ rights, with justices set to decide whether Colorado can require Catholic preschools that receive public funding to admit children of same-sex couples.

Colorado’s universal preschool program funds 15 hours of weekly preschool for a child, but the school must agree to provide families an “equal opportunity” to enroll regardless of various conditions, including sexual orientation and gender identity.

The Archdiocese of Denver, two Catholic parishes with preschools and parents of preschool-age children, say Colorado violated their First Amendment right to religious liberty by refusing to grant them an exception. The state says the same rules apply to every institution that accepts public funding.

The case could have broader implications for publicly funded religious institutions.

▪ The Hill : Judge dismisses case against ex-FBI agents in Hunter Biden probe.

HALEY’S CONSEQUENCES : House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.) said party members will consider “next steps” for how to address Rep. Haley Stevens ‘s (D-Mich.) surprise endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers when Congress returns next week.

“Haley Stevens made a terrible decision, blindsided everyone and isolated herself from the House Democratic Caucus,” Jeffries told Politico on Monday.

Some party members have reportedly called for Stevens to be punished or even kicked out of the caucus over her backing of Rogers in Michigan’s Senate race over El-Sayed. Stevens’s decision came as tensions between her and El-Sayed worsened but still came as a major shock to her fellow Democrats.

Party members have widely condemned the move and reiterated their support for El-Sayed.

▪ The Hill : The Memo: Michigan chaos may preview clashes ahead.

▪ The New York Times : Inside the El-Sayed-Stevens meltdown.

The president will meet with U.S. Ambassador to Portugal John Joseph Arrigo at 1:30 p.m. He will attend an election night viewing reception at 7 p.m.

National Guard troops control a street near a closed intersection where President Trump was holding an event, in Washington, Sept. 8, 2026. (J. Scott Applewhite, Associated Press)

ON GUARD : National Guard troops will play some role around midterm election security today in at least seven states.

Guard members in plain clothes will help monitor ballot boxes in seven Washington state counties; monitor and defend election networks in Iowa; and assist with election cybersecurity in Colorado, among other examples, The Hill’s Ellen Mitchell reports .

Federal law doesn’t allow armed personnel to be stationed at a place where an election is being held, unless there is an attack on a polling location and federal force is needed. But governors have increasingly called on their National Guard troops to monitor cybersecurity and assist local officials, Mitchell reports.

Seven states have publicly acknowledged the Guard playing a role in their midterms.

Meanwhile, Democrats have expressed concern that the Trump administration may use the military or immigration officers to intimidate voters at the polls, contest results or seize voting machines. The Department of Homeland Security has said it doesn’t plan to send immigration officers to the polls.

The Guard remains deployed in Washington, D.C. and will patrol on Election Day. City officials have asked for the placement of troops near mail ballot drop boxes to be limited.

▪ The New York Times : Election security agency retreats ahead of midterms.

▪ CNN : Election officials brace for foreign threats.

A woman holds an Iranian flag as part of a pro-government campaign in downtown Tehran, Iran, Oct. 26, 2026. (Vahid Salemi, Associated Press)

DEAL OR NO DEAL: The U.S. military struck radar detectors and missile launchers on Iran’s Qeshm Island on Monday.

“This was a defensive measure for Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against U.S. assets,” a U.S. official told NewsNation .

The strike came just a day before the midterms as new questions are arising over Trump’s next steps in Iran.

Regional experts tell The Hill’s Filip Timotija and Laura Kelly that the president appears to be leaning toward military escalation in the short term over reaching a potential deal with the Middle Eastern country.

“That seems to be where Trump is headed,” Eric Brewer , deputy vice president for the Nuclear Materials Security Program at the Nuclear Threat Initiative said in an interview with The Hill on Monday.

Jonathan Ruhe , a fellow for American Strategy at the Jewish Institute for National Security of America, said all signs point to the conflict resuming, noting Trump seems to think there is a “short war” option to achieve a “decisive” result.

“Trump’s most effective strategy against the Iranians is this longer-term and more patient but painful economic warfare strategy with the blockade and the aggressive sanctions,” Ruhe told Timotija and Kelly.

Mediators have been pushing both countries to reach a deal to end the war, with Qatar leading the push for renewed talks, backed by Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey. Even Vice President Vance sent a letter to Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei last week, according to The Wall Street Journal, in an effort to revive peace negotiations.

Trump has predicted that, once the midterms are behind him, the war in Iran will quickly come to its conclusion, but he has not been clear on how that would happen.

“The ball is in the U.S. court, because our demands have been stated very clearly and transparently, and Iran’s demands are reasonable and logical,” Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei told reporters Monday in Iran.

▪ The Hill : Iran offers to open Strait of Hormuz on several conditions.

▪ The Hill : Volodymyr Zelensky warns Russia could exploit midterms to launch attack.

The 119th Congress did more by making government do less , Rep. Lisa McClain (R-Mich.) writes in The Hill.

Democrats ready for blame game, whatever actually happens today , The Hill’s Chris Stirewalt writes .

Bill Murray performs at the 10th annual Love Rocks NYC concert benefiting God’s Love We Deliver at the Beacon Theatre on March 5, 2026, in New York. (Evan Agostini, Invision, Associated Press)

And finally … Actor Bill Murray stole the show Monday when he walked onto the set of CNBC’s “Squawk Box” to interrupt an interview with Trump’s top economic adviser, Kevin Hassett .

“Why is that man always smiling?” Murray asked as anchor Becky Quick handed him a microphone.

Hassett responded that his smile is because he’s thinking about Murray and that he’s a fan of Murray’s film, “Groundhog Day.” The actor said he’s “concerned — not worried — but concerned” about Hassett’s consistent grin.

Anchor Joe Kernen proposed that Hassett’s smile may be due to last week’s economic data , which showed the economy grew by 3.4 percent last quarter.

articles.title: Religious accommodations are a right, not a favor
articles.summary: Every morning, like so many other Americans, I kiss my son and husband goodbye and leave for work. But unlike many Americans, that ordinary routine depends on accommodations. My ability to practice law was contingent on the bar exam being presented to me in a format a blind applicant could use. Without accommodations, I would…
articles.body:
Every morning, like so many other Americans, I kiss my son and husband goodbye and leave for work. But unlike many Americans, that ordinary routine depends on accommodations.

My ability to practice law was contingent on the bar exam being presented to me in a format a blind applicant could use. Without accommodations, I would not have my job as an appellate lawyer. I would not have clerked at the U.S. Supreme Court and might not even be raising a family.

The accommodations that have allowed me to fully pursue my education and to participate in civic life have made all the difference.

The Supreme Court is now facing a similar issue in a case that will be argued this morning, St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy. The case, brought by my law firm, the Becket Fund for Religious Liberty, is about whether Colorado may legally exclude Catholic preschools from a tuition assistance program worth around $6,300 per year for children in pre-K.

Although the case is about religious-freedom protections, there is a connection to the law of disability accommodations. Colorado allows schools to participate in its preschool funding program if they prioritize and accommodate children with particular disabilities (like blindness or deafness). But schools that similarly prioritize and accommodate children with certain religious beliefs — like Catholic or Evangelical preschools — are excluded. Disability, Colorado says, merits special solicitude, but religious beliefs merit a flat denial.

Disability, Colorado says, merits special solicitude, but religious beliefs merit a flat denial.

The government draws an artificial line between the limits of the body and the limits of the soul. As a blind Catholic, the boundaries of my conscience are just as unchangeable as the limitations of my vision. I am just as incapable of counseling a client to end a human life as I am of reading a printed page.

Americans have long recognized that society ought to meet both those with disabilities and those with religious beliefs where they are. The Declaration of Independence promised Americans an “equal station” because “the Laws of Nature and of Nature’s God entitle them” to those rights. All men and women are created equal, even if we don’t always do the best job recognizing that principle in practice.

As preeminent legal scholar Michael McConnell has explained , accommodations are sometimes required to ensure that all are treated fairly. This is one area where disability and religion have principles in common. Examples of disability accommodations include ramps, closed-captioning, and Braille signage. Examples of similar religious accommodations might include providing kosher food for observant Jewish servicemembers, not scheduling Seventh-day Adventists to work on their Saturday Sabbath, or allowing Muslim or Sikh firefighters to wear beards. During wartime, including during the American Revolution itself, Quakers and other pacifists were allowed to serve their country in alternative ways instead of bearing arms. During Prohibition, there was an exception for sacramental wine.

These accommodations are not indulgences. They are not favors. They are something we have always done to ensure that we as a nation honor everyone’s human dignity. We recognize the constraints imposed on our fellow Americans and work together to ameliorate, overcome, or accommodate them — even when it costs us something in the process.

In St. Mary, Colorado wants to give dignity to some Coloradans but not others. Although the state rightfully supports accommodations for deaf or blind children, it refuses to do so for children and families whose Catholic faith limits their preschool options to institutions committed to honoring their values. In fact, the state refuses to do so, even while acknowledging that Catholic preschools are shutting down — thus eliminating preschool options for many Catholic families.

But human dignity is not a favor that Colorado may bestow on those it likes and deny to those it does not. Rather, it is fundamental to what it means to be a full member of society.

Religious accommodations, like disability accommodations, are rights, not favors. That means Colorado has to recognize and honor the human dignity of all its citizens, including those whose religious beliefs it rejects.

Laura Wolk Slavis is counsel at the Becket Fund for Religious Liberty .

articles.title: Do you need an ID to vote? Maybe not, in these states
articles.summary: Found yourself at the polls but don’t have your wallet? Depending on where you live, you may still be able to vote.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – Found yourself at the polls but don’t have your wallet? Depending on where you live, you may still be able to vote.

In most states, you are going to need a form of identification – the most common being a driver’s license or a voter ID card – before you can cast your ballot.

Here’s what to know before you vote on Election Day.

Which states do not require an ID to vote?

The District of Columbia and 12 states do not require voters to show identification before casting their ballot.

As of Oct. 2026, those states include California , Illinois , Maine , Maryland , Massachusetts , Minnesota , Nevada , New Jersey , New Mexico , New York , Pennsylvania , and Vermont .

Generally speaking, as long as residents of the above states are registered to vote and have voted at their polling place before, they won’t need to show an ID.

If they are registering to vote, they do have to submit at least one form of identification when registering to vote. First-time voters will likely need to provide identification to a poll worker before they can cast a ballot, even if they registered before Election Day.

What qualifies as identification, and how many forms of identification you need to provide, can vary. In DC, for example, you can use a valid driver’s license, a student tuition bill, or a residential lease. Local election officials do recommend that DC residents bring “some form of identification with you to vote in case you need it.” In New Jersey, a store membership card , including a Costco card, is acceptable.

In most other states, voters need a photo ID to cast their ballots.

Even without a photo ID, you may still be able to cast a provisional ballot in these states, as long as your identification can otherwise be confirmed. That’s permitted in Alabama , where you can also vote without a photo ID if you are “positively identified by two election officials as a voter on the poll list who is eligible to vote and the election officials sign a sworn affidavit so stating.”

While they do not require a photo ID to vote in Michigan , “voters in possession of a photo ID must present it at the polls.” Those without an acceptable form of ID can sign an affidavit saying they don’t have it with them and be allowed to vote. Texas has a similar rule for its voters.

If a voter in Iowa forgot their ID, another registered voter can attest for them. Both will have to sign an oath.

Alaska , Colorado , Connecticut , Delaware , Virginia , West Virginia , and Wyoming will accept IDs that do not have a photo. Generally, you will need to have registered to vote ahead of time, and that process may require a photo ID.

Arizona will accept either one photo ID, two forms of identification with a current address, or a photo ID and a form with a current address on it. Montana will accept a photo ID or other forms of identification that list a voter’s name and current address.

States that primarily vote by mail have slightly different requirements. In Hawaii , all registered voters automatically receive a ballot in the mail. To register, they need to provide a driver’s license or state ID and Social Security number. Oregon voters do not require a photo to register to vote, while Utah does, or two forms of alternative IDs.

While Washington is also primarily a vote-by-mail state, those who want to vote in person need to provide identification or sign a ballot declaration.

This guidance could have been much different had the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) America Act been enacted earlier this year.

The House passed the SAVE Act in February, but it stalled in the Senate in June. In response, President Trump canceled signing bipartisan housing legislation , saying he wouldn’t sign it until the SAVE Act passed. He later conceded the SAVE Act was “probably not going to happen.”

Had it passed, registering to vote would require additional documentation, like a passport or birth certificate. Republicans said the legislation was needed to prevent voter fraud, but Democrats warned it would disenfranchise millions of Americans by making it harder to vote.

articles.title: On this Election Day, and in the days to come, get ready to defend your vote
articles.summary: If Trump’s favored candidates are defeated at the ballot box, we should expect him to try to bring some of them victories in any way he can.
articles.body:
This Election Day is a pivotal moment for millions of people who worry that the American Dream is slipping out of reach as they struggle to pay for gas, groceries, utilities, healthcare and other necessities.

An NBC News poll published in October found that 71 percent of Americans believe our country is on the “wrong track.” Polls also show President Trump’s job approval rating is below 40 percent, with voters opposed to his corruption, incompetence, tariffs, war with Iran and other failed policies.

The president, who has repeatedly urged voters to act as though he is on the ballot, has motivated many Americans to vote for Democrats.

In a desperate bid to preserve Republican control of the House and Senate, regardless of voters’ wishes, Trump may disregard laws and the Constitution to try to overturn legitimate Democratic midterm victories.

If past behavior is any guide, Trump will claim without credible evidence that Democrats “ rigged ” elections, especially close races, and try to use federal power to put defeated Republicans in office. He knows that Democratic majorities would challenge his harmful policies and hold his administration accountable for abuses of power.

If Trump’s favored candidates are defeated at the ballot box, we should expect him to try to bring some of them victories in any way he can, because he is not simply opposed to Democrats; he’s opposed to democracy. He wants Republican candidates to win no matter how much damage he does to our 250-year-old system of representative government.

We saw Trump’s anti-democratic behavior when he refused to admit his loss in the 2020 presidential race to Joe Biden. Trump and his allies filed and lost 76 lawsuits seeking to overturn his defeat. Since he still denies his own loss six years ago, we should expect Trump to order the Justice Department and Republican groups to file lawsuits to challenge Republican losses in the midterms.

Trump has repeatedly ignored laws, the Constitution and ethical standards to corruptly monetize his office and pocket billions of dollars , slap his name on buildings and programs, seek to build a White House ballroom and a 250-foot-tall Triumphal Arch , roll back progress in civil rights and voting rights , cruelly deport hundreds of thousands of unauthorized immigrants and take many other harmful actions.

The president has also ignored the requirement for congressional approval of his senseless trade wars against nations around the world and his shooting war against Iran that he launched Feb. 28 . These wars have cost Americans billions of dollars and have created an affordability crisis that. Trump absurdly calls “a hoax.”

And tragically, members of our military have lost their lives, been wounded and suffered terrible hardships in the war with Iran that Trump told us would last “four to five weeks.”

Trump’s disastrous performance in office has given Democrats realistic hopes of midterm election victories in red states that have not sent Democrats to the House and Senate in many years.

While denouncing the Justice Department and New York state for prosecuting him after his first term, Trump has weaponized the department more than any other president to go after his enemies and try to help Republicans win midterm races.

Already, the Trump administration has challenged election results in Alaska’s Senate race if the Republican candidate loses and has challenged the right of up to 20,000 Californians and hundreds of people in Washington state to vote.

A federal judge in California issued a ruling Wednesday blocking the administration action there, writing that it endangered America’s democracy. A federal appeals court upheld the judge’s ruling Friday, and the Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration’s request to intervene Monday.

Now we face the frightening possibility of Trump using the FBI, Department of Homeland Security, the military and other parts of the U.S. government to confiscate voting machines and take other unprecedented and anti-democratic actions to overturn legitimate election results so Republicans can retain control of the House and Senate and win other races.

I realize these warnings sound alarmist. But if someone had predicted the Jan. 6, 2021 deadly riot at the Capitol by Trump supporters seeking to overturn his 2020 election defeat, most of us would have considered that prediction alarmist.

All this makes it vital for Americans who haven’t yet cast ballots during weeks of early and mail voting to vote on Election Day. Voting is a precious right that gives every American citizen the power to make elected officials work for our best interests, rather than their own, as Trump has done.

Continued Republican control of the House and Senate would give Trump the opportunity to amass more unchecked power and further weaken the guardrails of our democracy. The only way to stop him from causing additional harm is to elect a Democratic House and Senate that will impose long-overdue limits on his power grab and hold him accountable for all the harm he has caused our nation.

It’s our solemn duty as citizens to exercise our constitutional and hard-fought freedom to vote and to make our voices known to all, including Trump.

Donna Brazile is a political strategist, a contributor to ABC News and former chair of the Democratic National Committee. She is the author of “ Hacks: Inside the Break-ins and Breakdowns That Put Donald Trump in the White House .”

articles.title: The Movement: Conservatives make closing arguments against socialism
articles.summary: The final hours of the midterm season are upon us, and conservative groups fighting against the odds to preserve the Republican power trifecta in Washington are broadcasting their closing arguments, which equate Democrats with socialism, but are also bracing for a loss of power that seems more and more likely after the elections. “While we…
articles.body:
The final hours of the midterm season are upon us, and conservative groups fighting against the odds to preserve the Republican power trifecta in Washington are broadcasting their closing arguments, which equate Democrats with socialism, but are also bracing for a loss of power that seems more and more likely after the elections.

“While we hope Republicans maintain the House and the Senate, the results of election night don’t matter in the grand scheme of things,” said Douglas Blair , spokesperson for Heritage Action. “If Republicans win, we have to protect all the Trump admin’s accomplishments and follow through on a clear agenda to fix the American people’s concerns. If Republicans lose, conservatives will need to unite to protect the country from the radical, unapologetically socialist left.”

The anti-socialism push could stick as a defensive message for Republicans if they do lose their majority, much like anti-Trumpism has been a rallying cry for Democrats during their years out of power.

Bill Riggs , spokesperson for Americans for Prosperity Action, a conservative grassroots group tied to the Koch family, said mobilizing against socialism was a motivating factor for voters his group surveyed as Democratic Socialists of America-backed candidates began to pick up steam throughout the year.

“We saw warning signs this summer that 1 in 5 base Republican voters were at risk of either staying home or voting for the Democrat,” Riggs said. “Then the DSA agenda began to take hold on the left, and that opened the door to re-energizing those base voters and swing voters. That’s why our closing message is laser-focused on contrasting the harm of those socialist policies with a credible alternative to lower costs. That message has cut the at-risk Republican base in half, and it’s working in real time at the doors with swing voters.”

AFP Action’s last round of ads in Senate swing states centered around this approach, tying each Democratic candidate to the DSA’s policies whether or not that candidate aligns with them.

Senate Republicans, in a press release Monday, touted the accomplishments of the Republican-held Congress, including their signature tax cut legislation and progress on a bundle of conservative priorities like immigration enforcement, classically Republican ideals.

That list did not include some of Trump’s most prominent policies, including the Iran War and global tariffs. And some free-market conservatives noted that the GOP’s midterm approach bears more resemblance to the old-fashioned brand of Republicanism, at least in terms of economics, than it does to the tariff-happy, bigger-government agenda championed by Trump.

Trump, for his part, used a Monday speech to tout his renovations to D.C. landmarks like the Reflecting Pool, without much focus on the midterms beyond calling the Democratic candidates “extreme” and “the most dangerous candidates ever put up.”

He also repeated his promise to give $5,000 to every American if Republicans win, a proposal that blindsided congressional Republicans, who were generally opposed.

The Old-vs-New Right dynamic could be crucial for the next era of the Republican Party, either as it seeks to find its footing again after taking losses this year or charts a new majority era with the 2028 presidential primary on the horizon.

Republicans will need to unite around something, and the divisions in the party over economics, foreign affairs, family policy and countless other issues under Trump will need bridging on the path back to future power.

But those who want a restoration of traditional free-market, small-government conservatism are hoping their ideas have mass appeal that can course-correct the party. These closing arguments are evidence of that, they say.

“Despite countless keystrokes spent online, the so-called New Right’s arguments are almost completely absent from the Republicans’ closing message,” said Jonah Wendt, spokesperson at Advancing American Freedom. He mentioned the GOP ads during NFL games on Sunday that dug into the low-tax, free-markets approach, emphasizing a contrast between Republicans who will “cut your taxes” and Democrats who “will raise them.”

“With as much data as they could possibly have, campaigns, Super PACs, consultants and ad makers turned to traditional conservatism to make the case for voters to give the GOP a second chance,” Wendt added.

WILL REPUBLICANS KEEP THEIR LEADERS IN A MINORITY?

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) is signaling he’s not planning on leaving his leadership role — or Congress — anytime soon.

That’s unusual. Typically, Republican leaders who lose their majority have stepped down and out of the body. But Johnson has hinted that he’ll bid again to be leader, even in a Republican minority, Trump has suggested he endorses the move .

His colleagues aren’t sure Johnson will go through with it, though, after three grueling years as Speaker when he struggled to unite a restive GOP conference and navigate a minefield of Trump policies, like the Iran War, that are unpopular even with many Republicans. Not to mention, his conference would still have to elect him.

“There’s certainly a lot less trappings and a lot less power, and also the caucus just tends to kind of want to clean some house. Like members just see it as an opportunity to just switch things up,” GOP strategist Amy Frederiksen told my colleagues Sudiksha Kochi and Mike Lillis .

The looming question of where Johnson will go will hang over the post-midterm leadership shuffle, especially if Democrats perform as well tonight as polls and analysts expect. Reps. Steve Scalise (R-La.) and Jim Jordan (R-Ohio), original candidates for Speaker in the race that elected Johnson, have downplayed their interest in the job but other sources told Sudiksha and Mike that both are privately angling for it.

If Republicans lose their majority, the blame could fall on Johnson, especially if there’s a blue landslide. But generally, Republican sources said Johnson was well-respected and had been seen as running a strong show amid a chaotic two years with razor-thin margins.

Meanwhile in the Senate, there’s little doubt that Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) will run for another term, as he has said he plans to, even if Republicans lose the majority. He’ll also probably win.

Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), who lost to Abdul El-Sayed in the Democratic primary for Senate in Michigan, endorsed the Republican candidate, former Rep. Mike Rogers , over the weekend. It’s a stunning role reversal in a campaign cycle where many Republicans of all stripes have endorsed Democratic candidates for Senate, including GOP governors in Kansas and South Carolina . More here .

House Republicans are deploying staff around the country to add oversight to elections in battleground districts. The program runs every cycle, but this year’s is set to be “the most robust” as Republicans seek to hold onto their House majority. More here .

After the midterms come the lame-duck floor fights over what to prioritize, and it’s looking less likely that a reconciliation bill packed with GOP priorities will get across the finish line. Senate GOP aides threw cold water on that possibility, even while some Republicans in both the House and Senate are eager to stay in through the holidays to get it done. More here .

November 10-12: Conservative groups including Heritage, The Claremont Institute and the Conservative Partnership Institute gather at The Forum, a new national conference for conservatives featuring a range of speakers, including Scott Jennings , James Braid , Nick Freitas and Spencer Pratt . Details here .

November 18: The Foundation for Research on Equal Opportunity hosts Freedom & Progress 2026, a gathering of leaders committed to expanding opportunity through free enterprise, innovation, pluralism, and individual liberty. Details here .

articles.title: Rising cost of living tops voters’ concerns as midterm ballots cast
articles.summary: The rising cost of living and dissatisfaction with President Trump are the top concerns for nearly half of voters heading into Tuesday’s midterm elections, according to a new survey. The Reuters/Ipsos poll, released late Monday, found that 48 percent of registered voters ranked the cost of living as the most important factor in deciding their…
articles.body:
The rising cost of living and dissatisfaction with President Trump are the top concerns for nearly half of voters heading into Tuesday’s midterm elections , according to a new survey.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll , released late Monday, found that 48 percent of registered voters ranked the cost of living as the most important factor in deciding their vote, far outpacing concerns about democracy, at 26 percent, and immigration, at 13 percent.

The findings highlight the economic frustrations facing Republicans as they fight to maintain control of Congress amid difficult political terrain. Many Americans reported that their household finances have deteriorated since Trump returned to the White House.

Nearly half of Americans, 49 percent, said their financial situation has worsened during Trump’s second term, compared with just 13 percent who said it has improved. Another 37 percent reported little change, the data shows.

The economic pessimism was particularly strong among Hispanic respondents, with 54 percent saying their finances had worsened under the Trump administration, while just 10 percent reported an improvement.

Americans have also grappled with higher fuel prices tied to the unpopular U.S.-Israeli war with Iran — which entered its eighth month heading into the elections, adding to broader concerns about affordability.

The national average price for a gallon of gas sits at $4.15 as of Tuesday morning, according to AAA , up more than a dollar from a year ago.

The Iran conflict itself has also become a political liability for the president. Just 25 percent of voters said the military operations against Iran have been worth their costs, compared with 55 percent who said they have not. Another 18 percent were unsure, the survey found.

The cost of the U.S.’s war against Iran has risen to $47 billion — up $3 billion from September — with the biggest chunk of the cost going to munition replacement.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll was conducted online among 1,765 U.S. adults ahead of Election Day. It has a margin of error of 2 percentage points.

articles.title: America’s report on human trafficking takes a massive step backward
articles.summary: It slashed information relating to extraterritorial child sexual exploitation, child sexual abuse material, male sex trafficking victims, the LGBTQ community, non-governmental organizations, and, shockingly, trafficking survivors.
articles.body:
Since 2000, the annual Trafficking in Persons Report has been the government’s most effective tool to combat human trafficking worldwide. The report objectively diagnoses countries’ successes and shortcomings, recommending concrete changes to improve things.

Since 2010, the report has held the U.S. to the same standards. However, the 2026 report takes a massive step backward, eliminating all of its prioritized recommendations and slashing coverage of governments’ shortcomings in combating human trafficking. This year’s report, which was released more than three months late, comes in the wake of last year’s mass layoffs and prodded early retirements that decimated the State Department’s trafficking office to barely a quarter of its former size.

This year’s report eliminated all of its nearly 2,000 prioritized recommendations across 188 countries. Those recommendations were the report’s engine, telling other governments what to fix and providing a yardstick for measuring their progress. Without prioritized recommendations, the report is a shell of itself.

The 2026 report also cut nearly 40 percent of the content in the previous year’s report . It slashed information relating to extraterritorial child sexual exploitation, child sexual abuse material, male sex trafficking victims, the gay and transgender communities, non-governmental organizations, and, shockingly, trafficking survivors.

The report doesn’t just evaluate foreign governments’ efforts to combat trafficking; it also evaluates U.S. government efforts to do so. This year’s U.S. section is roughly one-third the length of last year’s. It no longer contains recommendations. Last year , there were 14.

The critical findings of nongovernmental organizations and survivors are gone. The Jeffrey Epstein case, which galvanized public opinion on child sex trafficking, is omitted entirely, including the virtually unanimous enactment of the Epstein Files Transparency Act in November 2025 and the Justice Department’s botched partial disclosure of trafficking evidence.

Instead, the first accomplishment the new report cites for the U.S. in combating trafficking is “strengthened immigration enforcement at the border.” Numerous organizations, including my organization, Protect All Children from Trafficking , have underscored how mass-deportation efforts have put child trafficking survivors at risk.

What the report leaves out matters more than what remains. Last year’s U.S. narrative acknowledged anti-trafficking experts’ concerns about trafficking victims facing deportation without being identified. It noted that the government had canceled the contract providing legal services to unaccompanied children and that processing times for T-visas , which offer trafficking victims an opportunity to temporarily stay in the U.S., had grown to nearly 15 months.

This year, those alarms have disappeared, along with statistics on T-visas and continued presence temporary designations — protections that encourage foreign-national trafficking victims to come forward.

The report accurately notes that federal funding for victim services provided by nongovernmental organizations fell from $82.3 million to $18.9 million, a 77 percent cut, and that funding for youth trafficking prevention education dropped by nearly a quarter since last year. But it fails to describe the impact of those cuts.

There is also genuine progress worth recognizing. Federal trafficking convictions rose from 210 to 293 , and the Trafficking Survivors Relief Act became law, giving survivors a federal path to clear convictions for crimes they were forced to commit. But a report that celebrates enforcement while staying silent on collapsing victim services is not an honest assessment.

In February, Protect All Children from Trafficking submitted recommendations to the State Department for this year’s U.S. narrative. The first was to treat prevention education as a pillar. Our review of 15 U.S. anti-trafficking curricula found that not one was designed primarily for K-12 students or parents. Second, recognize the transportation sector as a front line for prevention. Third was to address the vulnerability of boys, who are routinely undercounted and underserved. Fourth was to require real survivor leadership in designing prevention programs. And the final recommendation was to reckon honestly with how immigration enforcement is undermining victim identification.

Little of this made it into the report. On the bright side, prevention education earned a few sentences in a state-level sidebar focusing on Florida’s HB 1237 , which mandates human trafficking awareness training across the public school system, and a funding figure that revealed a dramatic cut in prevention education funding.

On the negative side, boys got one sentence. Transportation workers appear only in a list of people who received training. Survivor involvement was reduced to the fact that an advisory council met. On immigration, the report did not merely ignore our concerns; it perversely reframed the harsh enforcement as a signature anti-trafficking achievement.

Next year, the State Department should ensure that the Trafficking in Persons Office’s size and stature are restored to ensure it has the personnel and resources to produce a candid and thorough report, including prioritized recommendations, and support those recommendations with robust diplomatic and foreign-assistance engagement.

Congress has a role, too. Through oversight hearings and the next reauthorization of the Trafficking Victims Protection Act, lawmakers can insist that the report remain the rigorous, evidence-based assessment they intended. They can restore funding for victim services and prevention education, and ensure unaccompanied minors have legal representation.

The United States led the creation of the playbook against human trafficking. A shorter Trafficking in Persons Report that goes easier on ourselves and allies does not make children safer. It only makes their exploitation easier to ignore.

Aram A. Schvey is senior director of Policy and Government Relations at Protect All Children from Trafficking and previously served as Senior Congressional Advisor in the State Department’s Office to Monitor and Combat Trafficking in Persons.

Democrats are seeing a narrow lead as voters head to the polls Tuesday, according to a new survey.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll , released Monday, found that 46 percent of registered voters said they would back Democrats in congressional races, compared with 38 percent who favored Republicans. That margin narrowed from an 11-point Democratic advantage in a similar poll conducted a week earlier.

Meanwhile, President Trump’s approval rating remains underwater. The data shows just 32 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s job performance. That is unchanged from last week and 1 point above the record low of 31 percent recorded in October.

Trump also appears to be a motivating factor for some independent voters , with 50 percent saying they view their congressional vote as a vote against the current administration. Just 13 percent said they were voting in support of the president, while another 33 percent said he would not influence their decision.

His low approval rating comes amid growing frustration over the cost of living , driven in part by rising fuel prices as the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran continues ahead of Election Day.

The national average price for a gallon of gas sits at $4.15 as of Tuesday morning, according to AAA , up more than a dollar from a year ago.

Affordability concerns and dissatisfaction with the president’s agenda were top of mind for voters heading to cast their ballots.

articles.title: Full appeals court to rehear case on Trump administration election worker threats
articles.summary: The full 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals voted late Monday to rehear the Trump administration’s appeal of a lower court order that blocked it from threatening election workers with criminal prosecution if they do not set aside ballots suspected to have been cast by noncitizens. The decision came hours after a divided three-judge panel…
articles.body:
The full 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals voted late Monday to rehear the Trump administration’s appeal of a lower court order that blocked it from threatening election workers with criminal prosecution if they do not set aside ballots suspected to have been cast by noncitizens.

The decision came hours after a divided three-judge panel lifted a restraining order issued by U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson, allowing the Justice Department to resume its demands to states.

Chief Judge Mary Murguia, an Obama appointee, wrote in a late-night order that the panel’s decision was vacated after a majority of the court’s nonrecused active judges voted to rehear the case en banc.

Two labor unions and political interest groups sued the Trump administration last week after the Justice Department sent letters to California and Washington requesting the states check their voter rolls for potential ineligible voters and sequester those mail ballots until citizenship status can be verified. One of the letters sent to Los Angeles officials warned of “significant federal scrutiny and legal exposure” if they did not comply.

The challengers accused the administration of unlawfully trying to interfere with the midterm elections by attempting to coerce election officials with threats, arguing it could disenfranchise lawful voters.

Appeals Court Judges Carlos Bea and Consuelo Callahan, both George W. Bush appointees, found that the government was likely to succeed on the merits. The judges wrote in a majority opinion that the Justice Department’s actions fell within the scope of “core Executive functions” that did not “actually disturb” the states’ constitutional right to administer their elections or violate federal voting rights law.

“We therefore decline Plaintiffs’ invitation to read the VRA [Voting Rights Act] as rendering the Executive’s exercise of those functions as unlawfully intimidating, threatening, or coercive,” the seven-page majority opinion read.

Murguia dissented, writing that the majority’s holding in the case “cannot be reconciled” with an earlier 9th Circuit decision that rejected the Trump administration’s bid to set aside 20,000 California ballots. The chief judge wrote that the executive branch had “no right” to dictate election procedures to the states.

“And if Defendants cannot dictate these procedures directly, then they likewise cannot dictate them by subjecting vulnerable election workers to baseless—but chilling—threats of federal prosecution,” the judge wrote. “The Constitution’s allocation of election procedures to the states is meaningless if Defendants can coerce states into foregoing their chosen procedures by abusing their prosecutorial powers.”

The Supreme Court earlier on Monday turned away the Trump administration’s emergency request to segregate the California ballots.

articles.title: Do you need to vote in every race on your ballot?
articles.summary: So-called “undervoting” is permitted.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – After months of campaigning, Election Day has finally arrived. If you didn’t take advantage of early voting options, it’s now time to head to your polling place and cast your ballot.

You may, though, find yourself being asked to vote in a race you haven’t been following or on a ballot measure you don’t have a desire to weigh in on.

If that’s the case, you do not have to vote for a candidate or option in either section. You can instead leave it blank and vote in other sections. This would be considered an “undervote,” meaning you voted in fewer races, appointments, or amendment questions than you were permitted to vote in.

Whether you vote in one race or all but one contest on your ballot, it will be counted.

Alabama election officials tell voters they are “not required to vote in all races on the ballot,” explaining , “participation is your choice.” Many other states, including Colorado , Iowa , and Georgia , offer similar guidance.

If you would rather write in a candidate than vote for one already on the ballot, it may or may not be allowed.

Maryland , for example, warns that write-ins are accepted in a general election but not a primary election. Louisiana does not allow write-ins.

If you aren’t sure what you will be voting for on Election Day, you can find sample ballots on USA.gov , though they will not include information about the candidates.

articles.title: Remote work is here to stay
articles.summary: Remote work grows when workers reward it and employers gain confidence running it.
articles.body:
A new hire logs in from a kitchen table in Phoenix, joins a standup with teammates in Austin and Bogotá, ships work by lunch, and closes the day with customer calls across three time zones.

That routine feels ordinary today, because the tools matured and the norms settled, and because leadership at some organizations rewards output over presence. Evidence from a new working paper ties that lived reality to company age and CEO age — and it points toward a future with more remote opportunity than today.

Remote work expands through structure, not vibes. Younger companies keep forming and scaling, and their operating systems tend to include distributed hiring and flexible schedules from the start. Younger CEOs keep moving into decision seats, and they carry a management style built around digital collaboration, written clarity and measurable outcomes. Those two trends reinforce each other, and they create a labor market where more professionals can build serious careers without living near a headquarters.

The study from the National Bureau of Economic Research shows that workers average more work-from-home days per week under CEOs in their twenties than under CEOs in their sixties, a signal that younger leaders more often choose flexibility as a deliberate operating strategy.

Younger executives often build trust through systems rather than sightlines. They rely on dashboards, clear metrics and shared documentation instead of hallway visibility. That approach fits remote work because it centers accountability and reduces ambiguity. It also aligns with what many workers already expect from modern employers.

Young companies often treat flexibility as a default setting because they start with fewer legacy routines and fewer sunk costs in office space. The NBER analysis finds that employees at firms founded after 2015 work from home far more often than employees at firms founded before 1990, and the gap remains large even after accounting for other differences between workers and firms.

That matters because young firms bring fresh job creation and expansion into the economy, and their internal rules shape what becomes normal for hiring. When those firms scale, their early choices harden into standard practice. A founder who builds around cloud tools, asynchronous documentation and distributed recruiting keeps hiring outside headquarters years later, because the system already works.

Flexibility also removes a growth constraint: geography. Teams that recruit nationally fill specialized roles faster and broaden their candidate pool beyond a single metro region. That advantage compounds in competitive labor markets. Research on job amenity value shows that many workers place meaningful value on flexible arrangements, which helps remote-friendly firms attract strong applicants even when pay looks similar.

For professionals, that shift changes where opportunity lives. High-growth firms increasingly resemble networks rather than buildings. People who communicate well in writing, manage time zones smoothly, and deliver crisp outcomes become easy to hire from anywhere, and that creates more remote roles at every level.

Remote work also holds steady at a meaningful level across the U.S. economy, which gives CEOs cover to keep flexibility in place. Leaders learn how to run distributed teams, employees learn how to collaborate asynchronously. Vendors build better tools. Those capabilities spread from tech into finance, health care administration, professional services, and industrial supply chains, because coordination problems look similar across sectors.

Remote work grows when workers reward it and employers gain confidence running it. Worker preference remains strong in remote-capable roles, and that preference shapes retention and recruiting outcomes. Ongoing polling on remote work preferences shows sustained demand for hybrid arrangements, and employers respond when hiring gets harder and turnover gets expensive.

Job postings confirm the same pattern. Analysis of remote postings based on large-scale job ads shows remote and hybrid shares rising sharply during the pandemic and staying well above pre-2020 levels afterward.

Taken together, the direction stays clear. Young companies keep scaling with remote-friendly defaults. Younger CEOs keep rising and formalizing those defaults into durable policy. Workers keep choosing flexibility when they can, and employers keep meeting that demand because it improves recruiting reach and strengthens retention.

Remote work will keep expanding because the companies that grow fastest increasingly operate that way, and the leaders who gain influence increasingly prefer it. That combination opens doors for millions of workers who want a bigger job market, more control over location, and a career that rewards outcomes. The office will remain a tool, remote work will remain a pathway, and the share of people who can choose that pathway will keep rising.

Gleb Tsipursky, Ph.D., serves as the CEO of the future-of-work consultancy Disaster Avoidance Experts and wrote “ The Psychology of AI Adoption at Work: From Resistance to Results ” and “ ChatGPT for Leaders and Content Creators .”

The chances of Democrats taking the House are as good as 96 percent, the Harvard model forecasts. According to the model, the chances of Republicans winning the…
articles.body:
Recently updated election models from Harvard University forecast a strong chance of Democrats winning a majority of seats in the House and the Senate in the midterm elections.

The chances of Democrats taking the House are as good as 96 percent, the Harvard model forecasts . According to the model, the chances of Republicans winning the House are “as likely as rolling a 20 on a twenty-sided die.”

“Our forecast expects the underdog to win with these odds once in about 26 elections. The last time an underdog won with similar odds was 1952,” researchers wrote.

The Democrats need 218 seats to take the House and, by Harvard’s models, 186 seats are labeled safe, 36 are considered likely and nine lean toward Democrats. The model predicts 10 seats as toss-ups.

The overall projection, by this model, stands at 242 Democratic seats in the House.

Even though the odds are slightly lower than in the House, the Democrats still have a 78 percent chance of taking the Senate, according to Harvard .

To win the Senate majority, a party would need 51 seats, and the current overall projections from Harvard forecast 53 Democratic seats in the Senate.

Out of the 35 Senate races happening this year, seven have been labeled as competitive races. Races in Texas, Ohio, Kansas and Alaska are in the “Lean Democrat” category while South Carolina and Nebraska are in the “Lean Republican” category.

The model shows the Iowa Senate race as a toss-up.

The model presents five scenarios of predictability along with historical polling errors. These include if the polls are correct, normal polling error favoring Democrats or Republicans and historic polling error favoring either party.

“Since 1950, the median polling error is 2 points in either direction, and 3 of the 19 midterms have had an error within 0.5 points,” according to the forecast.

articles.title: Trump says US will cut off $4B in aid to Israel, blames bad ‘talking point’
articles.summary: President Trump said on Tuesday that he has reached a deal with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that will end U.S. aid to Israel this year.
