articles.body:
President Trump said on Tuesday that he has reached a deal with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that will end U.S. aid to Israel this year.

Trump said in an interview with “Fox & Friends” that he and Netanyahu made a deal “months ago” for Washington to end its aid to Israel.

“They’re fine with it,” the president said. “They’ve become a very successful country. They don’t need it, and we won’t be paying anymore.”

Trump noted the U.S. would “help” Israel if they need it, noting the Middle Eastern country has been “a great ally.”

The development would mark a major shift in U.S. foreign policy. Israel is considered one of the largest recipients of U.S. foreign aid, which is authorized by Congress.

Netanyahu told CBS News in May that he would like to gradually reduce Israel’s reliance on U.S. military aid over the next 10 years.

“I want to draw down to zero the American financial support, the financial component of the military cooperation that we have. Because we receive $3.8 billion a year. And I think that it’s time that we weaned ourselves from the remaining military support,” Netanyahu said.

“I said, let’s start now and do it over the next decade, over the next 10 years, but I want to start now. I don’t want to wait for the next Congress. I want to start now,” the prime minister said when asked if he had a specific time frame in mind.

Splits over U.S. policy toward Israel, including military aid, have opened in both parties amid the war in Gaza.

Trump’s comments on Tuesday come as voters in the U.S. head to the polls for Election Day.

While affordability is a top concern for voters, the issue of Washington’s support of Israel amid the war in Gaza has influenced some key races, including Michigan’s contentious Senate race.

Trump referred to Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed’s criticism of Israel in the interview on Tuesday.

“Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like El-Sayed when they don’t need it? It’s a bad talking point,” the president noted.

Polls show that a growing number of Americans say that U.S. aid to Israel should be rolled back or stopped altogether. According to a survey released earlier this month by the Chicago Council on Global Affairs, 21 percent of surveyed Americans said U.S. military aid to Israel should be decreased, and 35 percent said it should be ended altogether.

articles.title: The Trump administration needs to get serious about publishing abortion data
articles.summary: The CDC has published its annual abortion surveillance series since 1969 — that is, it did until 2025.
articles.body:
Senate confirmation hearings are often filled with vague promises and deflective answers. But this was not the case when now-Director Erica Schwartz of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention declared, “Senator, you have my commitment. “ She was affirming that data collection on abortion is a critical component of her agency’s work.

For the sake of women and their healthcare providers, Director Schwartz must keep to her word.

National abortion data collection is older than Roe v. Wade itself. As states began to liberalize their abortion laws in the late 1960s, the CDC established the Abortion Surveillance System to track abortion-related maternal mortality and morbidity, collect demographics of abortion-seeking populations, and monitor unintended pregnancies.

Voluntary state reporting measures were rightfully deemed necessary public health controls. These only became associated with anti-abortion efforts after women’s safety had been subordinated to abortion access by the abortion legalization movement.

The CDC has published its annual abortion surveillance series since 1969, traditionally in late November. Despite known underreporting , this series is critical for informed consent practices, allowing women and their providers access to the full scope of risks associated with abortion when making decisions about their pregnancy.

But for the first time since the series outset, the CDC failed to publish this report in 2025 , citing agency cutbacks. This missed report notably was to include abortion surveillance from 2023, the first year following the Dobbs decision. That year is especially important because the shifting landscape of abortion law in the fallout of Roe had not settled by the end of 2022. State restrictions were subject to ongoing litigation, and many laws faced immediate injunctions.

Abortion providers have also shifted increasingly toward telehealth dispensing models , circumventing state-level laws intended to curb national abortion numbers. Surveillance from 2023 will offer a first picture, however blurred or incomplete, that women will have into abortion risk post-Dobbs.

Unfortunately, as recent news suggests , failure to provide timely reports on abortion safety seems to be a theme for this administration. Both sides of the abortion debate, and the mainstream media, are focused heavily on the Food and Drug Administration’s review of the medication abortion drug, mifepristone, and the continued delay of public results until next March. But this disregard of more than half a century of longitudinal abortion data collection is also a departure from the administration’s “Gold Standard Science” maxim and raises questions about the commitment to its own transparency standard.

Director Schwartz, even aside from the commitment she made in her confirmation hearing to Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.), must prioritize the release of this post-Dobbs data and ensure the 2026 report is released on time.

Public health is a service to the populace. Data cannot be withheld for fear it will be weaponized by ideologues. Although federal abortion policy has increasingly become a data war, surveillance informs regulatory action to protect women from potential harms. To hide data is to force women to make decisions in the dark.

Moreover, although Congress alone has the authority to mandate federal reports from the states, but that does not leave the CDC without responsibility to provide the states with a top-down standard that reflects what patient-deidentified elements should be reported.

In the era following Dobbs, where medication abortions comprise nearly two-thirds of all abortions, the CDC should request that states volunteer specifications that enable intergovernmental accountability for compliance with the drug’s use. To ensure compliance with federal drug regulations, states should also track and report the serial and lot numbers for abortion drugs prescribed along with drug expiration dates.

And even in states where abortion shield laws protect out-of-state prescribers from criminal and civil penalties for mailing abortion drugs to women in states where it is illegal, the CDC should request that states record the abortion providers who prescribe the drugs, the prescriber’s state, and whether the medication abortion was completed at the provider’s facility or at home — of course keeping all patient information confidential.

Public health organizations are not political pawns. Schwartz must not forfeit the CDC’s commitment to data transparency, or to the women and healthcare providers it informs.

Gavin Oxley is director of external affairs and media strategy for Americans United for Life .

articles.title: The dangerous loophole turning U.S. attorney’s offices into political instruments
articles.summary: In February 1897, all criminal prosecutions in the District of Columbia stopped. Trials were postponed. New arrestees unable to post bond faced indefinite detention. A wanted fugitive captured in another state could not be extradited. For 22 days, no prosecutorial authority existed in the nation’s capital. The cause of this disruption? The absence of a…
articles.body:
In February 1897, all criminal prosecutions in the District of Columbia stopped. Trials were postponed. New arrestees unable to post bond faced indefinite detention. A wanted fugitive captured in another state could not be extradited. For 22 days, no prosecutorial authority existed in the nation’s capital.

The cause of this disruption? The absence of a U.S. district attorney (as today’s U.S. attorneys were then called).

On Feb. 6, 1897, the term of the incumbent, Arthur A. Birney, expired. A few days before, the lame-duck president, Grover Cleveland, had nominated the head of the local bar association, Henry E. Davis, to succeed Birney. However, the Senate declined to act on the nomination. When Birney left office, no statute clearly provided for the appointment of an interim district attorney for the capital.

Without a Senate-confirmed official or any mechanism for the appointment of an interim, it was understood that there was no place for the prosecutorial power to reside. The stalemate ended only after Congress passed legislation permitting the local federal court to appoint an interim district attorney; President Cleveland reluctantly signed the bill. On March 1, days before Cleveland left office, the Senate voted down Davis’s nomination, and the judges of the local court appointed the failed nominee to serve in an interim capacity — something he would do for the following two-and-a-half years.

This now-forgotten episode has new relevance.

Presently, 10 of the country’s 93 U.S. attorneys’ offices are leaderless. Contrary to the command of a federal statute , in these districts, there is no presidentially appointed and Senate confirmed U.S. attorney. Moreover, there is no lawfully serving interim or acting official.

Congress provided that when U.S. attorney vacancies go on for long enough, it is up to the district court to appoint an interim prosecutor. This administration has circumvented that provision by repeatedly firing the court-appointed attorneys (despite the president’s authority to do so being legally dubious, at best). These offices serve a combined population of roughly 43.2 million people, meaning about 12 percent of all Americans live in districts lacking a chief federal law enforcement officer.

Unlike in 1897, the 10 offices have not closed. Instead, each office is being led by a first assistant U.S. attorney, despite there being no statutory basis for such an arrangement. This is usually a senior career government attorney. Several of those leading the 10 offices at issue do not fit this mold — seven are political actors brought in from outside of government. The administration has used this loophole to install its chosen picks to lead these U.S. attorneys’ offices, bypassing the check of Senate confirmation.

In an upcoming article for the Wake Forest Law Review , I contend that the 1897 view should prevail: without a U.S. attorney, assistant U.S. attorneys lack the power to litigate on behalf of the government. Congress has vested prosecutorial power in the attorney general and the U.S. attorneys; assistant U.S. attorneys must derive their authority from one of those two sources.

Today’s Justice Department takes the view that the powers of the roughly 6,300 assistant U.S. attorneys come directly from the attorney general. This position renders U.S. attorneys superfluous — figureheads who can be dispatched without consequence.

But why does this matter? Because the long tradition of quasi-independent U.S. attorneys’ offices, responsive to the needs and values of their communities, is being eroded. Although supervised by the attorney general, as fellow presidential appointees, U.S. attorneys have long been afforded wide latitude to make individual prosecutorial decisions (within the administration’s policy parameters). Those offices led by assistant U.S. attorneys are entirely beholden to the attorney general. This arrangement permits political actors to micromanage the offices for political purposes.

There are costs to adhering to the formalistic view adopted in 1897, of course. But given the overtly political actions taken by this Justice Department, do the harms caused by disruption really outweigh those caused by a lack of accountability?

In 1897, it took only three weeks for Congress and the president to act. It could be that withdrawing power from these leaderless assistants today would spur the nomination and confirmation of qualified individuals who can be trusted to fairly exercise the vast federal prosecutorial power.

Jonathan S. Ross is a visiting assistant professor of law at the University of South Carolina’s Joseph F. Rice School of Law. He previously served as the acting and court-appointed interim United States Attorney for the Middle District of Alabama.

articles.summary: Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) has no regrets after endorsing the Republican nominee for U.S. Senate in Michigan, former Rep. Mike Rogers. When asked by NewsNation, The Hill’s broadcasting partner, whether endorsing Rogers was worth the backlash, Stevens said it “absolutely” was. “Absolutely,” Stevens said while headed to vote in Birmingham, Mich., alongside her mother. “Voting…
articles.body:
Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) has no regrets after endorsing the Republican nominee for U.S. Senate in Michigan, former Rep. Mike Rogers.

When asked by NewsNation , The Hill’s broadcasting partner, whether endorsing Rogers was worth the backlash, Stevens said it “absolutely” was.

“Absolutely,” Stevens said while headed to vote in Birmingham, Mich., alongside her mother. “Voting is always worth it, right?”

Despite her choice to endorse a Republican in the Senate race, the congresswoman said she still wants Democrats to have a majority in the House, with Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) as Speaker.

“You know what this is? It’s the people’s day,” Stevens added. “And I told this to our next Speaker of the House, Hakeem Jeffries. It’s majority-makers day.”

Stevens has been widely criticized by her own party for her endorsement of Rogers, which stemmed from a feud with Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, whom Stevens lost to in the primary.

El-Sayed and Stevens were set to make a joint appearance at a Detroit church with Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-S.C.), but after Stevens asked El-Sayed to apologize for an ad run by an outside progressive group blaming Israel for rising gas prices, El-Sayed uninvited her from all of his campaign events.

The next day, Stevens appeared at church alongside Rogers, not El-Sayed.

Democrats slammed the move , which was a sharp reversal from Stevens’s initial public support for El-Sayed.

“Haley Stevens made a terrible decision, blindsided everyone and isolated herself from the Democratic caucus,” Jeffries told Politico on Monday.

Curtis Hertel, chair of the Michigan Democratic Party, said Stevens was no longer a member of the party and would not be going forward. Some of Stevens’s own staff resigned over her Rogers endorsement.

However, if Stevens’s endorsement of Rogers was meant to help him, it may not be enough to move the needle in the final stretch of the campaign.

While few polls of the race have been conducted since Stevens’s endorsement of Rogers, a New York Times/Siena University poll released over the weekend showed El-Sayed ahead by 11 points.

Decision Desk HQ, a partner of The Hill, gives El-Sayed a 75 percent chance to retain the seat for Democrats.

Most polls in Michigan close at 8 p.m. EST, but results come in slowly . An analysis from nonpartisan election news site Votebeat shows that Michigan did not reach more than 50 percent of its counted vote until after midnight in 2024 — more than four hours after polls closed.

articles.title: In search of the real Dan Sullivan
articles.summary: A controversy erupted in Alaska following allegations that the Peltola campaign attempted to recruit a namesake candidate to confuse voters during the Senate primary, leading to legal challenges and investigations that ultimately failed to overturn the election results.
articles.body:
Thank God! This has been such a boring campaign season. Nobody arrested, no candidates breaking down in tears, no known Russian interference. We needed a real scandal to shake it up.

And now we’ve finally got one! Well, not a big scandal — just a teeny-weeny scandal. But it’s just enough to make this last week more colorful. And more than enough to drive President Trump crazy. Of course, I’m talking about Alaska’s Dan Sullivans. Both of them.

It all started on Aug. 18, when 16 candidates appeared on Alaska’s non-partisan Senate primary ballot, including incumbent Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, running for reelection, and former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola. Under Alaska’s “ranked-choice voting” rules, the top four candidates advanced to the Nov. 3 general election ballot.

When votes were counted , Peltola came in first, winning by 8 points. Sen. Sullivan came in second. Third and fourth place went to two other Republicans: Gerald L. Heikes and yet another Dan Sullivan: Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr., a retired schoolteacher.

Senator Sullivan’s campaign immediately cried “foul,” accusing Peltola staffers of recruiting schoolteacher Sullivan to run, only to confuse voters. The Peltola campaign denied any involvement. Daniel J. Sullivan insisted he decided to file on his own and, in response to a lawsuit filed by Sen. Sullivan, the Alaska Supreme Court ruled that the “other” Sullivan had every right to run.

That kind of settled things until last week, when the New York Times dropped a bombshell . Its dogged investigative reporters exposed a plot by the Peltola campaign to hunt down anyone named “Dan Sullivan” and convince him to run against Sen. Sullivan — yes, only in order to confuse voters. The Peltola campaign and Daniel J. Sullivan himself had been lying.

That’s when the stuff hit the fan. The Republican governor of Alaska launched an investigation . Trump called on Peltola to drop out of the race. And, on Trump’s orders, the Justice Department filed an unusual lawsuit demanding that Alaska invalidate results of the Nov. 3 Senate election — but only if Senator Sullivan lost. That “Hail Mary” pass also failed this past weekend, when a federal judge dismissed DOJ’s case as unenforceable.

At least for now, that marks the end of the “big, beautiful,” Alaska Senate scandal — which, in the end, proved to be not such a big deal, after all. Much ado about nothing.

To start with, recruiting someone with the same name as your opponent to run for the same office in order to confuse voters may be a political dirty trick. But it’s not illegal. It’s wrong. But, if anything else, it’s stupid, not illegal. Because you might get caught and embarrassed, like the Peltola campaign has been.

Nor is this the first time it’s been tried. It’s an old trick used by both Democratic and Republican politicians. Most recently, in 2024, Washington state’s Democratic Attorney General Bob Ferguson ran for governor. He was challenged on the ballot by not one, but two other Bob Fergusons — both Democrats and both recruited by his Republican opponent in order to confuse voters. The scheme failed.

In fact, in my research, I could not find one case of a “same-name” lesser candidate winning or changing the outcome of any election. It won’t happen in Alaska, either, because the Alaskan people are smarter than that.

It may be cold up there. Alaskans may be busy with jobs and family. But they can still read and write. Looking at the official senate ballot, they can easily tell the difference between Sen. Sullivan — listed as “Dan S. Sullivan, incumbent, Republican” and retired schoolteacher Dan Sullivan — identified only as “Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr.” — with no given political party or occupation. There’s no doubt which is which, and Alaskans know it. No matter what President Trump says, if Senator Sullivan loses to Peltola, he can’t blame it on the other, unknown Dan Sullivan.

You must also admit, it’s rich to hear Trump complain about any effort to “confuse voters.” This is man who still claims he won more popular votes than Hillary Clinton in 2016, who still refuses to admit he lost the 2020 election to Joe Biden, and who filed 62 lawsuits alleging voter fraud in 2020, nearly all of which were dismissed for lack of evidence.

When it comes to confusing voters, Trump is the master, not Daniel J. Sullivan of Petersburg, Alaska.

articles.title: New York attorney general says office monitoring ballot scanning issue in Westchester
articles.summary: Voting machines across polling sites in Westchester County, N.Y., experienced widespread problems Tuesday after ballot scanners stopped accepting votes, according to state officials. New York Attorney General Letitia James (D) sought to reassure voters after the mishap. “My office is monitoring this issue with scanners in Westchester and is in touch with the state and…
articles.body:
Voting machines across polling sites in Westchester County, N.Y., experienced widespread problems Tuesday after ballot scanners stopped accepting votes, according to state officials.

New York Attorney General Letitia James (D) sought to reassure voters after the mishap. “My office is monitoring this issue with scanners in Westchester and is in touch with the state and local Boards of Elections as they work on a solution,” she wrote on the social platform X .

“Westchester voters can still safely fill out and turn in their ballots at their polling locations,” James continued. “Your votes will count.”

The problems began when polls opened at 6 a.m., affecting polling locations throughout the county, Westchester County executive Ken Jenkins confirmed.

In a statement Tuesday, the Westchester County Board of Elections said an issue involving paper ballots was preventing some machines from accepting ballots, though the precise cause of the malfunction remains unclear.

“The Westchester Board of Elections wants to reassure every voter that your vote matters, your ballot will be secure, and your vote will be counted,” the board said.

Officials instructed voters to continue filling out the papers, which will be placed in designated orange emergency ballot bags if they cannot be processed by the scanners. The ballots will be secured and counted later, they added.

The New York State Board of Elections also noted that the technical difficulties did not prevent residents from casting their ballots.

“Long-established emergency ballot procedures have been implemented, where completed ballots are secured, under bipartisan control, and will be counted,” the state board said in a statement.

Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.), who is facing a competitive reelection bid in New York’s 17th Congressional District, said the problem appeared to affect every ballot scanner in the county.

“We do not yet know the exact cause of the issue, whether it is the ballot or the machine,” he said on X .

“The Board of Elections is working with their vendors to resolve it,” he added, urging voters to remain at their polling locations and cast their ballots.

articles.title: Dirty Democratic political tricks abound
articles.summary: The article argues that Democrats have employed various controversial political tactics during the current election cycle, including alleged ballot stacking in Alaska and Montana and previous strategic spending patterns.
articles.body:
Democrats’ concerns about a growing threat to democracy — 85 percent in a recent Pew Research Center survey — would be more believable if they weren’t so actively engaged in political dirty tricks that undermine the democratic process. Their recent antics in the Alaskan Senate race may be the dirtiest in this election cycle, but there are others.

A New York Times investigation alleges that Alaskan Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola, who represented Alaska in the U.S. House of Representatives from 2022 to 2025, and her campaign operatives worked with the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee for months to find an Alaskan with the same name as the current Republican incumbent, Sen. Daniel S. Sullivan. And they found one: Dan J. Sullivan, who was allegedly persuaded to run as a Republican, but switched to “undeclared ,” for the U.S. Senate. He denies the allegation .

Alaska’s multiparty, ranked-choice voting system allowed the alternative Sullivan to make it to the general election. The Democrats’ apparent plan was to confuse voters in order to draw votes away from the incumbent Senator Sullivan, giving the victory to Peltola. Fortunately, the state has taken steps to ensure voters know which Sullivan is the incumbent Republican.

The Times explains that both Republicans and Democrats have engaged in “ ballot stacking ” — that is, persuading other, often unknown, candidates to run for office to draw votes from one of the leading candidates.

For example, the Wall Street Journal reports that in a 1998 U.S. House race in Georgia, Republicans ran a candidate named John H. Lewis, Jr., against the famed civil rights leader and Democratic incumbent Rep. John Lewis. But that was a Republican against a Democrat — it didn’t fool Democratic voters. The Democrat Lewis won in a landslide.

Both Peltola and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee reportedly deny any involvement in recruiting the alternative Sullivan. But the Times investigation undermines that denial, shining a very awkward light on Democratic tactics.

That’s not the only instance of dirty Democratic tricks this election season. Montana is a very red state , and Democrats were looking for their best chance to beat the Republican candidate, Kurt Alme, a former U.S. attorney who’s running for an open U.S. Senate seat.

The Democratic candidate is Alani Bankhead, a woman of color, a retired Air Force lieutenant colonel and federal agent. As Bankhead told her story to This American Life , she had little money and support until positive ads started appearing, along with mailers and social media. She had no contact with or knowledge of the political action committee sponsoring the ads.

The ads greatly boosted her image, and she easily won the Democratic primary. Then the ads stopped, cold turkey. She didn’t know why.

It turns out that there’s an independent also running for the Senate seat — Seth Bodnar, a West Point graduate, former veteran and, importantly, president of the University of Montana.

Bankhead believes Democrats helped her win the nomination with the goal of getting her to drop out of the race so Democrats would back the independent, Bodnar. He is considered a moderate and the best option for beating Alme.

If that was the Democratic plan, it failed, even though there was a major public push to get her to drop out. Bankhead says she is the Democratic nominee and has no intention of dropping out. So far, the Republican candidate is leading in the polls .

Another dubious Democratic practice, which we mostly heard about in 2022, was Democrats spending millions of dollars backing far-right MAGA Republican candidates in their primaries. The goal was to get the most unelectable Republicans to win their primaries so the Democratic candidates would have an easier road to win in the general election.

The Washington Post reported on the practice in 2022, along with providing some of the ads. According to the Post, “Democrats have spent money to help a trio of further-right candidates win primaries in governor’s races in Illinois, Maryland and Pennsylvania.” They also used the strategy, unsuccessfully, in certain races in California and Colorado.

The Post says that some ads sound like attacks that the candidate was too conservative. But that was meant to draw the most conservative voters to those candidates, undermining any more traditional Republican candidates.

Of course, the dirtiest trick belongs to the 2016 Clinton campaign’s funding of the now-discredited “Steele dossier .” In 2022 the Federal Elections Commission fined the Democratic National Committee and the Clinton campaign $113,000 after it “found ‘probable cause to believe’ that both the campaign and national party ‘misreport[ed] the purpose of certain disbursements,’” according to Politico .

The recent tactics in Alaska and Montana may not be illegal, but they are slimy and cynical. Republicans at the state and federal levels are investigating. Sadly, the actions open the door for even more dirty tricks by both parties at a time when the last thing most voters want is dirtier politics.

Merrill Matthews is the Texas state chair of Our Republican Legacy.
